A few years ago, I was wallowing in emotional and physical burnout, trying to adjust to life outside of the African village we had called home for eight years. Depression and fear were a regular part of my life. As I slowly crawled out of the hole I was in a hole I never realized I had fallen into until it was too late for an easy remedy, I began to notice beauty.

In those intense years of ministry and language learning in the village, spending time on beauty seemed like a waste of time. And honestly, we lived in a village with very little beauty to offer, the only brightness being the vibrantly colored clothing the women wore. The mud houses, the flat landscape, and dust everywhere were daily life for most months of the year. Though I'm a lover of peace, quiet, and beautiful things, I made very little space in my life for any of it, even the things I could have done in that environment.

We now live in an easier place; the Southern Highlands of Tanzania. Here, there is fresh air and sunshine the whole year long. Flowers... of all kinds, and a lovely house with smooth floors and freshly painted walls. And it's now that I realize how important beauty is to the soul and how important it is to actually notice the beautiful things in my life and create beauty at every possible moment.

Being a mother and homemaker, no matter where in the world God has placed us, is a beautiful thing in itself if we really see it for what it is. It's easy to complain about the daily mundane things that make up my life, the constant dust, or the fact that I'm cooped up in our compound week after week. But I have been surprised with joy. Here are a few things I love to do to keep life fresh and inspiring:

Writing

I especially like to write about the goodness and faithfulness of God. True joy comes from Him, not my circumstances. I’ve believed that for years, but it’s just recently that I’ve actually experienced this reality. My focus is so easily honed in on the things that I wish would be different, thinking that without the uncertainty and difficulties, I’d be happy. I now realize that difficulties have very little to do with the amount of joy found in my heart. Instead, we can allow difficulties to teach us what true joy is and where it comes from.

Keeping a reasonably clean, pleasant house

I try to get rid of the extras and replace the dirty, the dingy, and the ugly with something that is beautiful and lovely. Get rid of the limp, ugly curtain in the schoolroom and replace it with a fresh yellow one (yes, even if it does take a few dollars to do so, I remind my penny-pinching soul).

Clearing off all horizontal surfaces

One of my goals is to clean off all flat surfaces in my house and leave only pleasant, tasteful things. I function so much better if my house is a restful, orderly place. Even though with five children, restful and orderly are relative terms, I’m learning that the rush and mess and noise of a family are beautiful too. It makes the clean floor all the more amazing and thankworthy because it’s a rare experience.

Doing something fun with my children

I like to plan something fun to do with my children, such as a fun science project or an outing. Our favorite is outings to the flower gardens, which are grown here in town along the roadside as a showcase to give other people ideas of how to grow and care for flowers. Tucked into corners here and there, I find all the common flowers I was used to seeing in the States. It’s delightful and even more fun when some of the children share my love for growing things.

Serving food tastefully

Even rice and beans can be served in pretty bowls instead of the messy pots they were cooked in. Raid your local market and you will be surprised with what you can find in glassware and other beautiful dishes that brighten your table.

Speaking cheerfully

Speak cheerfully—to the laundry lady, the house helper, or the neighbor. I can't spend a lot of time in ministry with people other than my children, but there are always people coming around that I can touch with a smile, kindness, or any help they need. It's easy to be peeved over the fact that the produce vendor can't remember NOT to come in the morning while I'm teaching school, and her voice at the door interrupts us again. And what do math facts, bread dough, and dirty floors really have to do with joy? How does the noise of life and cantankerous personalities blend with the eternal? It’s all mixed up in my heart, often with the dusty realities on top and threatening to spill over, but if I give in to peevish attitudes, that is a true joy killer.

Spending time appreciating the beauty of nature

This rests my mind and draws my heart to God. Though I've never lived in the Garden of Eden or places of equal beauty, there's always something to notice, something as small as a patch of green grass struggling to survive the dry season (which is a season of trial for me here in this country). It’s cold (45 degrees or colder in the morning). The green growth and refreshing rains are over. Everything green is dying or has long been dead. Even the house roofs have lost their color as the dust covers every possible surface and threatens to suffocate the inspiration out of humans as well. Even the mountain in view from my kitchen window has lost its beautiful patchwork of gardens and fields. It stands bare and sober, waiting with bated breath for rain—just like my heart. But I’ve delighted in one little patch of earth in our back yard that I keep watered. There are peace lilies, roses, hibiscus, and other bright flowers blooming, and succulents growing in delightful little pots. I lug heavy buckets of water to that spot and sometimes take all five of my children on the city buses to visit yet another flower garden in search of more flowers. It’s not a waste of time for me, as that little spot in my backyard during this dry season refreshes my heart over and over again!

Practicing gratefulness

With a very busy husband, I don’t have a lot of time with him, and he doesn’t have a lot of carefree time with the children. However, I’m making it a habit to notice the small things that do happen, like looking out my kitchen window and seeing him sitting on a mat with the girls, just enjoying them. I stand and watch, thanking God for that moment. It could have gone unnoticed, especially if my heart was full of peevish ungratefulness. Noticing the tiny flashes of joy throughout my day eventually makes my life seem full of joy, though in reality, my life has plenty of trials and challenges.

Life here in town is easier in so many ways, but we’ve been bombarded with many challenges working with the government, which has consumed Tim’s time and energy. Even though we hadn’t lived in the village for over four years, we were doing a lot of support work for our fellow missionaries there and making trips back to where we still felt was our home. But all of us have been banned from that village and have had to work hard to even obtain the necessary documents needed to simply stay in the country.

Recently our compound in the village was taken over by the local army, just weeks after two Tanzanian missionary families moved in. When Tim traveled back to communicate and to hand over the keys out of respect for the ones who were forcing us to do this, he was insulted with hours of irrational anger and mistreatment, along with a lot of demands. Of course, our hearts were broken about seeing our house used for army training rather than for those precious new missionary families who were leaving their homes in town in order to take on the work there.

My husband is exhausted, both physically and emotionally, yet this morning he left for another trip back to the village to “heap on coals of fire” by giving the angry army officer a solar panel and a transformer on top of the other things he demanded. It’s our reasonable service. And yes, my heart had tears in it as I stood at the window and watched him go. I know that he’s only subjecting himself to more mistreatment, and that hurts my heart. But I also know that it’s only through these things that God teaches me joy. As I surrender things dear to my heart, I’m emptied of my own desires. There’s nothing to hang on to anymore and nothing to fight for. So, there’s plenty of room for God to fill my heart with what he wants in there—Joy.

Yes, life hasn’t brought a lot of serendipity my way. There have been a lot of tears, but that’s not my focus anymore, as I purposefully bring beauty into every possible crevice of my life and delight in the surprise of joy. My quest is to allow my home and this tiny space on this earth to be a place where God’s kingdom comes. It can’t be all about happy things, peace, and serendipity, because that isn’t given to me. It’s got to be all about something really good going on in my heart and how that affects everything that my hands touch. My heart can be declaring the works of the Lord as I see him using trials in my life to build my faith and the faith of others looking on. In that way His kingdom comes into this small place, in this little crevice of life, in this space, empty of inspiration, except for His amazing grace, which turns trial into joy.

For noen år siden lå jeg i emosjonell og fysisk utbrenthet, og forsøkte å tilpasse meg livet utenfor den afrikanske landsbyen vi hadde kalt hjem i åtte år. Depresjon og frykt var en fast del av livet mitt. Mens jeg sakte krabbet meg ut av hullet jeg befant meg i — et hull jeg aldri innså at jeg hadde falt i før det var for sent for en enkel løsning — begynte jeg å legge merke til skjønnhet.

I de intense årene med tjeneste og språklæring i landsbyen virket det å bruke tid på skjønnhet som bortkastet tid. Og ærlig talt bodde vi i en landsby med veldig lite skjønnhet å tilby; det eneste lyset var de livlig fargede klærne kvinnene bar. Leirhusene av leire, det flate landskapet og støvet overalt var dagliglivet i store deler av året. Selv om jeg elsker fred, stillhet og vakre ting, ga jeg svært lite plass i livet mitt til noen av dem, selv ikke de tingene jeg kunne ha gjort i det miljøet.

Nå bor vi et enklere sted; Sørhøydene i Tanzania. Her er det frisk luft og solskinn hele året. Blomster... av alle slag, og et hyggelig hus med glatte gulv og nyleggete vegger. Og det er nå jeg innser hvor viktig skjønnhet er for sjelen, og hvor viktig det er faktisk å legge merke til de vakre tingene i livet mitt og skape skjønnhet ved enhver mulig anledning.

Å være mor og hjemmeværende, uansett hvor i verden Gud har plassert oss, er i seg selv noe vakkert hvis vi virkelig ser det for hva det er. Det er lett å klage over de daglige, trivielle tingene som utgjør livet mitt, det konstante støvet, eller det at jeg sitter innestengt i leiren vår uke etter uke. Men jeg har blitt overrasket av glede. Her er noen få ting jeg elsker å gjøre for å holde livet friskt og inspirerende:

Å skrive

Jeg liker spesielt å skrive om Guds godhet og troskap. Sann glede kommer fra Ham, ikke fra omstendighetene mine. Det har jeg trodd i mange år, men det er først nylig at jeg virkelig har erfart denne realiteten. Fokuset mitt fanger seg så lett på ting jeg skulle ønske var annerledes, og jeg tenker at uten usikkerhet og vanskeligheter ville jeg være lykkelig. Jeg innser nå at vanskeligheter har veldig lite å gjøre med hvor mye glede som finnes i hjertet mitt. I stedet kan vi la vanskeligheter lære oss hva sann glede er og hvor den kommer fra.

Å holde et rimelig rent, trivelig hjem

Jeg prøver å kvitte meg med det overflødige og erstatte det skitne, slitte og stygge med noe som er vakkert og herlig. Fjern den slappe, stygge gardinen i skoleværelset og erstatt den med en frisk gul en (ja, selv om det koster noen få dollar, minner jeg min sparsommelige sjel om det).

Å rydde av alle horisontale flater

Et av målene mine er å tørke av alle flate overflater i huset og la bare hyggelige, smakfulle ting stå igjen. Jeg fungerer så mye bedre hvis huset mitt er et hvilende, ordnet sted. Selv om med fem barn er hvilende og ordnet relative begreper, lærer jeg at fart, rot og støy fra en familie også er vakkert. Det gjør det rene gulvet enda mer fantastisk og takknemlig fordi det er en sjelden opplevelse.

Å gjøre noe morsomt med barna mine

Jeg liker å planlegge noe morsomt å gjøre med barna mine, for eksempel et artig naturfagsprosjekt eller en utflukt. Favoritten vår er utflukter til blomsterhagene, som her i byen er dyrket langs veikanten som en utstilling for å gi folk ideer til hvordan man kan dyrke og ta vare på blomster. Gjemt i kroker her og der finner jeg alle de vanlige blomstene jeg var vant til å se i USA. Det er herlig, og enda morsommere når noen av barna deler min glede for å dyrke ting.

Å servere mat smakfullt

Selv ris og bønner kan serveres i pene boller i stedet for de rotete grytene de ble kokt i. Ta turen til ditt lokale marked, og du vil bli overrasket over hva du kan finne av glassvarer og andre vakre fat som lyser opp bordet ditt.

Å snakke lystig

Snakk lystig—til klesvaskedamen, husassistenten eller naboen. Jeg kan ikke tilbringe mye tid i tjeneste for andre enn barna mine, men det er alltid folk som kommer rundt som jeg kan berøre med et smil, vennlighet eller den hjelpen de trenger. Det er lett å bli irritert over at grønnsaksleverandøren ikke klarer å la være å komme om morgenen mens jeg underviser, og stemmen hennes på døren avbryter oss igjen. Og hva har egentlig regneferdigheter, brøddeig og skitne gulv å gjøre med glede? Hvordan blander livets støy og kranglete personligheter seg med det evige? Alt dette er rotet i hjertet mitt, ofte med de støvete realitetene på toppen og truende om å renne over, men hvis jeg gir etter for grinete holdninger, er det en sann gledeforhinder.

Å bruke tid på å verdsette naturens skjønnhet

Dette hviler mitt sinn og trekker mitt hjerte til Gud. Selv om jeg aldri har bodd i Edens hage eller steder med tilsvarende skjønnhet, er det alltid noe å legge merke til, noe så lite som en flekk med grønt gress som kjemper for å overleve tørkesesongen (som er en prøvelsessesong for meg her i dette landet). Det er kaldt (45 grader eller kaldere om morgenen). Den grønne veksten og oppfriskende regn er over. Alt grønt dør eller har vært dødt lenge. Selv hustakene har mistet fargen ettersom støvet dekker enhver mulig overflate og truer med å kvele inspirasjonen hos menneskene også. Selv fjellet som er synlig fra kjøkkenvinduet mitt har mistet sitt vakre lappeteppe av hager og åkre. Det står bart og alvorlig og venter andpustent på regnet—akkurat som hjertet mitt. Men jeg har gledet meg over en liten jordflekk i bakgården som jeg holder vannet. Der blomstrer fredsliljer, roser, hibiskus og andre klare blomster, og sukkulenter vokser i herlige små potter. Jeg sliter med tunge bøtter med vann til det stedet og tar noen ganger med alle fem barna på bybussene for å besøke enda en blomsterhage i jakt på flere blomster. For meg er det ikke bortkastet tid, for den lille flekken i bakgården i denne tørkeperioden frisker opp hjertet mitt om og om igjen!

Å øve takknemlighet

Med en veldig travel ektemann har jeg ikke mye tid sammen med ham, og han har ikke mye sorgløs tid med barna. Likevel gjør jeg det til en vane å legge merke til de små tingene som skjer, som å se ut av kjøkkenvinduet og se ham sitte på en matte med jentene, bare nyte dem. Jeg står og ser på og takker Gud for det øyeblikket. Det kunne ha gått ubemerket hen, særlig hvis hjertet mitt var fullt av grinete utakknemlighet. Å legge merke til de små gledene gjennom dagen gjør etter hvert at livet mitt virker fylt av glede, selv om livet i realiteten har mange prøvelser og utfordringer.

Livet her i byen er på så mange måter enklere, men vi er blitt bombardert med mange utfordringer i arbeidet med myndighetene, noe som har slukt Tims tid og energi. Selv om vi ikke hadde bodd i landsbyen på over fire år, gjorde vi mye støttearbeid for våre medmisjonærer der og reiste tilbake til stedet vi fortsatt følte var vårt hjem. Men nå er vi alle blitt forbudt fra den landsbyen og har måttet arbeide hardt for å få nødvendige dokumenter bare for å kunne bli i landet.

Nylig ble leiren vår i landsbyen overtatt av den lokale hæren, bare noen uker etter at to tanzanianske misjonsfamilier flyttet inn. Da Tim reiste tilbake for å kommunisere og overlevere nøklene av respekt for dem som tvang oss til dette, ble han møtt med timer av irrasjonell raseri og dårlig behandling, sammen med mange krav. Selvfølgelig ble hjertene våre knust over å se huset vårt brukt til militærtrening i stedet for for de dyrebare nye misjonsfamiliene som forlot hjemmene sine i byen for å ta på seg arbeidet der.

Mannen min er utslitt, både fysisk og følelsesmessig, likevel dro han i morges tilbake til landsbyen for å "bære kull på hodet" ved å gi den sinte offiseren et solcellepanel og en transformator i tillegg til de andre kravene han stilte. Det er vår rimelige tjeneste. Og ja, hjertet mitt fyltes av tårer mens jeg sto ved vinduet og så ham gå. Jeg vet at han bare utsetter seg for mer dårlig behandling, og det smerter meg. Men jeg vet også at det er gjennom slike ting Gud lærer meg glede. Etter hvert som jeg overgir ting som står meg nær, blir jeg tømt for mine egne ønsker. Det er ingenting å holde fast ved lenger og ingenting å kjempe for. Så det er rikelig plass for Gud til å fylle mitt hjerte med det han vil ha der—Glede.

Ja, livet har ikke brakt meg mye tilfeldige gledesøyeblikk. Det har vært mange tårer, men det er ikke mitt fokus lenger, da jeg bevisst bringer skjønnhet inn i enhver sprekk av livet mitt og gleder meg over overraskelsen i gleden. Mitt mål er å la hjemmet mitt og dette lille rommet på jorden være et sted hvor Guds rike kommer. Det kan ikke bare handle om lykkelige ting, fred og tilfeldigheter, fordi det ikke er gitt meg. Det må handle om noe virkelig godt som skjer i hjertet mitt og hvordan det påvirker alt det mine hender rører ved. Hjertet mitt kan forkynne Herrens gjerninger når jeg ser ham bruke prøvelser i mitt liv til å bygge min tro og troen til dem som ser på. På den måten kommer hans rike inn i dette lille stedet, i denne lille sprekk av livet, i dette rommet, tomt for inspirasjon, bortsett fra hans bemerkelsesverdige nåde, som forvandler prøvelse til glede.

Artikkelen gjengis etter forespørsel. Den ble først trykt i The Heartbeat of the Remnant i høstutgaven 2019. Tidligere trykt i Earthen Vessels.

'Tis winter now; the fallen snow
has left the heavens all coldly clear;
through leafless boughs, the sharp winds blow,
and all the earth lies dead and drear.

And yet God's love is not withdrawn;
his life within the keen air breathes;
his beauty paints the crimson dawn,
and clothes each branch with glittering wreaths.

And though abroad the sharp winds blow,
and skies are chill, and frosts are keen,
home closer draws her circle now,
and warmer glows her light within.

O God, you give the winter's cold,
as well as summer's joyous rays,
you warmly in your love enfold,
and keep us through life's wintry days.

ha reso i cieli freddi e limpidi;

la sua bellezza dipinge l'alba cremisi,
e veste ogni ramo di corone scintillanti.

il focolare stringe ora il suo cerchio più vicino,

così come i raggi gioiosi dell'estate,
ci avvolgi calorosamente nel tuo amore,

“O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are His judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? Or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of Him, and through Him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen” (Rom. 11:33–36).

What an exuberant and expressive exclamation written by Apostle Paul! As we look at a new hymn and hymn writer again, let’s keep our minds alert and hearts open to see the hand of God at work.

Matthew Bridges was born at Malden, Essex, in England, on July 14, 1800. He began to publish verses in 1825 and continued until he had published two small volumes of hymns—Hymns of the Heart (1848) and The Passion of Jesus (1852). From here, I will continue with the story by giving a brief history of the church life of our hymnodist.

The hymn writer we are studying in this article was a part of the Anglican Church of England. Around the middle of the 19th century, he became dissatisfied with the church group he was with and found himself following the leading of John Henry Newman in what was called the Oxford Movement. According to hymnologist Albert Bailey, this movement centered on, “Claiming for their Anglican Church lineal descent from the original Apostolic Church.” In pursuit of this, the organization’s followers studied the ancient history of the church, its doctrine, and especially its liturgy. In doing so, they discovered a wealth of Greek and Latin hymnody from the earliest centuries of the Christian church.

As sadly, we find many factions in the Christian church today, so also was the scope of things going on in the mid–1800s. The Oxford Movement seemed in some ways to be a competition between the old and the new way of doing things. In the case of the figure in our story today, it seems he saw a more stable path forward in keeping the old traditions of the mother church, yet he also seemed to have a real, living faith in our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Now, I want to interject here that I trust his decision was made in all good conscience toward God, even though we look on today from an Anabaptist viewpoint and question his reasons for doing so.

We will continue with our story here. Matthew Bridges converted to Roman Catholicism and, wanting to share in the rich hymnic tradition of the Protestant Church, began writing original hymns. Mr. Bridges’ hymns are marked by spirituality and genuine power. One of his hymns we love and enjoy is “Rise, Glorious Conqueror.” Undoubtedly, his greatest hymn is “Crown Him with Many Crowns.” It first appeared in his book The Passion of Jesus, and was originally given the title “The Song of the Seraphs.”

There is an interesting background connected to this hymn, including how there came to be 12 verses. Understandably, only a portion of those verses are being sung today. The selection of verses depends on the hymnal.

Matthew Bridges originally penned the song in 1851. He wrote six stanzas, all based upon Rev. 19:12: “ ... and on His head were many crowns.” The edition by Bridges continued until the 1870s when a devout Anglican clergyman named Godfrey Thring came along. Godfrey was concerned that this popular hymn allowed catholic theology to be sung by protestant congregations. His concerns centered perhaps on Bridges’ original second verse, where he referenced the Blessed Virgin Mary. In light of this, Thring wrote six new stanzas and published it in his Hymns and Sacred Lyrics in 1874.

The 12 stanzas have been mixed and matched down through the years. Interestingly, of the six verses most commonly appearing in hymnals today, three were written by Bridges and three by Thring. The hymn, as published in the Hymns of the Church songbook, completely omits original verse 2 and uses verses 1, 3, 4, part of 5, and part of 6 out of Bridges’ original six verses. The stanzas we sing in that book are highlighted in the selection of verses below. Also included as well are the six couplets by Thring.

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Bridges

Crown Him with many crowns, the Lamb upon His throne;
Hark! how the heavenly anthems drowns all music but its own;
Awake, my soul, and sing of Him who died for thee,
And hail Him as thy matchless King through all eternity.

Crown Him the Virgin’s Son! The God Incarnate born—
Whose arm those crimson trophies won which now His brow adorn!
Fruit of the mystic Rose as of that Rose the Stem:
The Root, whence mercy ever flows—the Babe of Bethlehem!

Crown Him the Lord of peace! Whose power a scepter sways,
From pole to pole, that wars may cease, absorbed in prayer and praise:
His reign shall know no end, and round His pierced feet
Fair flowers of paradise extend their fragrance ever sweet.

Crown Him the Lord of love! Behold His hands and side—
Rich wounds, yet visible above, in beauty glorified:
No angel in the sky can fully bear that sight,
But downward bends his burning eye at mysteries so bright!

Crown Him the Lord of years! The Potentate of time—
Creator of the rolling spheres, ineffably sublime!
Glassed in a sea of light, where everlasting waves
Reflect His throne—the Infinite! Who lives—and loves—and saves.

Crown Him the Lord of heaven! One with the Father known,
And the blest Spirit, through Him given from yonder triune throne!
All hail! Redeemer—Hail! For Thou hast died for me;
Thy praise shall never, never fail throughout eternity!

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Thring

Crown Him with crowns of gold, all nations great and small,
Crown Him, ye martyred saints of old, the Lamb once slain for all;
The Lamb once slain for them who bring their praises now,
As jewels for the diadem that girds His sacred brow.

Crown Him the Son of God before the worlds began,
And ye, who tread where He hath trod, crown Him the Son of man;
Who every grief hath known that wrings the human breast,
And takes and bears them for His own, that all in Him may rest.

Crown Him the Lord of light, Who o’er a darkened world
In robes of glory infinite His fiery flag unfurled.
And bore it raised on high, in heaven—in earth—beneath,
To all the sign of victory o’er Satan, sin, and death.

Crown Him the Lord of life Who triumphed o’er the grave,
And rose victorious in the strife for those He came to save;
His glories now we sing Who died, and rose on high.
Who died, eternal life to bring and lives that death may die.

Crown Him of lords the Lord, Who over all doth reign
Who once on earth, the incarnate Word, for ransomed sinners slain,
Now lives in realms of light, where saints with angels sing
Their songs before Him day and night, their God, Redeemer, King.

Crown Him the Lord of heaven, enthroned in worlds above;
Crown Him the King, to whom is given the wondrous name of Love,
Crown Him with many crowns, as thrones before Him fall.
Crown Him, ye kings, with many crowns, for He is King of all.

Matthew Bridges lived his latter years in the province of Quebec, Canada, then returned to England before his passing from earth on October 6, 1894, at the ripe old age of 94. Although we don’t find many details about his life, he has left one of the greatest hymns in our hands today.

A great part of this song’s enduring quality is the tune it is paired with. This refrain was written especially for this song by Sir George Job Elvey in 1868 and was given the name of Diademata. In Greek, the word diademata means “a royal crown”—a fitting name for this stirring melody. Hymnology scholar J. R. Watson agrees with this when he observes, “Diademata makes a magnificent setting for the text, march-like and joyful without ever becoming mechanical or strident.”

May our congregations continue our practice of corporate, whole-hearted singing, lifting our voices in praise to the Lord in the assembly of the saints! Crown Him, our Lord Jesus Christ, with many crowns, for he is worthy!

«¡Oh profundidad de las riquezas tanto de la sabiduría como del conocimiento de Dios! ¡Cuán insondables son sus juicios, e inescrutables sus caminos! Porque ¿quién conoció la mente del Señor? ¿O quién fue su consejero? ¿Y quién le dio primero, y le será recompensado? Porque de él, y por él, y para él son todas las cosas. ¡A él sea la gloria por los siglos! Amén» (Rom. 11:33–36).

¡Qué exclamación tan exuberante y expresiva escrita por el apóstol Pablo! Al volver a ver un nuevo himno y un nuevo autor de himnos, mantengamos la mente alerta y el corazón abierto para ver la mano de Dios obrando.

Matthew Bridges nació en Malden, Essex, en Inglaterra, el 14 de julio de 1800. Comenzó a publicar versos en 1825 y continuó hasta haber publicado dos pequeños volúmenes de himnos—Hymns of the Heart (1848) y The Passion of Jesus (1852). A partir de aquí seguiré con la historia dando un breve repaso de la vida eclesiástica de nuestro himnógrafo.

El autor de himnos que estudiamos en este artículo formaba parte de la Iglesia Anglicana de Inglaterra. Hacia mediados del siglo XIX, se mostró insatisfecho con el grupo eclesiástico al que pertenecía y se encontró siguiendo la dirección de John Henry Newman en lo que se llamó el Movimiento de Oxford. Según el himnologista Albert Bailey, este movimiento se centraba en «reclamar para su Iglesia Anglicana el descendiente lineal de la Iglesia Apostólica original». En pos de esto, los seguidores de la organización estudiaron la historia antigua de la iglesia, su doctrina y, en especial, su liturgia. Al hacerlo, descubrieron una riqueza de himnografía griega y latina de los primeros siglos de la iglesia cristiana.

Así como tristemente hallamos hoy muchas facciones en la iglesia cristiana, también así era el alcance de las cosas que ocurrían a mediados de 1800. El Movimiento de Oxford pareció en ciertos sentidos una competencia entre la manera antigua y la nueva de hacer las cosas. En el caso de la figura de nuestra historia de hoy, parece que vio un camino más estable hacia adelante al mantener las viejas tradiciones de la iglesia matriz, sin embargo también parecía tener una fe real y viva en nuestro Señor y Salvador Jesucristo. Ahora, quiero intercalar aquí que confío en que su decisión fue tomada de buena conciencia ante Dios, aun cuando hoy miramos desde un punto de vista anabautista y cuestionamos sus razones para hacerlo.

Seguiremos con nuestra historia aquí. Matthew Bridges se convirtió al catolicismo romano y, queriendo participar de la rica tradición himnaria de la iglesia protestante, comenzó a escribir himnos originales. Los himnos del señor Bridges se caracterizan por su espiritualidad y auténtico poder. Uno de sus himnos que amamos y disfrutamos es «Rise, Glorious Conqueror». Indudablemente, su himno más grande es «Crown Him with Many Crowns». Apareció por primera vez en su libro The Passion of Jesus, y originalmente se tituló «The Song of the Seraphs».

Hay un trasfondo interesante conectado a este himno, incluyendo cómo llegó a tener 12 estrofas. Comprensiblemente, hoy solo se canta una porción de esas estrofas. La selección de estrofas depende del himnario.

Matthew Bridges escribió originalmente la canción en 1851. Compuso seis estrofas, todas basadas en Apoc. 19:12: «... y en su cabeza había muchas diademas». La edición de Bridges continuó hasta la década de 1870 cuando apareció un devoto clérigo anglicano llamado Godfrey Thring. Godfrey estaba preocupado de que este popular himno permitiera que la teología católica fuese cantada por congregaciones protestantes. Sus preocupaciones se centraban quizás en la segunda estrofa original de Bridges, donde hacía referencia a la Bienaventurada Virgen María. A la luz de esto, Thring escribió seis estrofas nuevas y las publicó en su Hymns and Sacred Lyrics en 1874.

Las 12 estrofas han sido mezcladas y combinadas a lo largo de los años. Curiosamente, de las seis estrofas que aparecen más comúnmente en los himnarios hoy, tres fueron escritas por Bridges y tres por Thring. El himno, tal como se publicó en el cancionero Hymns of the Church, omite completamente la estrofa original 2 y usa las estrofas 1, 3, 4, parte de la 5 y parte de la 6 de las seis estrofas originales de Bridges. Las estrofas que cantamos en ese libro están resaltadas en la selección de estrofas que sigue. También se incluyen las seis coplas de Thring.

Coronadle con muchas coronas

—Bridges

Coronadle con muchas coronas, el Cordero en su trono;
¡Escuchad! cómo los himnos celestiales ahogan toda música salvo la suya;
Despierta, mi alma, y canta de Aquel que murió por ti,
Y salúdale como a tu Rey incomparable por toda la eternidad.

Coronadle Hijo de la Virgen! El Dios Encarnado nacido—
¡Cuyos brazos obtuvieron aquellas trofeos carmesíes que ahora adornan su frente!
Fruto de la Rosa mística como del Tallo de esa Rosa:
La Raíz, de la cual brota siempre la misericordia—¡el Niño de Belén!

Coronadle Señor de la paz! Cuyo poder empuña un cetro,
De polo a polo, para que cesen las guerras, absortas en oración y alabanza:
Su reinado no conocerá fin, y alrededor de sus pies traspasados
Las flores del paraíso extienden su fragancia siempre dulce.

Coronadle Señor del amor! Ved sus manos y su costado—
Ricas heridas, aún visibles en lo alto, glorificadas en belleza:
Ningún ángel en el cielo puede soportar plenamente esa visión,
Pero inclina su ardiente mirada hacia abajo ante misterios tan radiantes.

Coronadle Señor de los años! El Potentado del tiempo—
Creador de las esferas que giran, ¡inefablemente sublime!
Espejado en un mar de luz, donde olas eternas
Reflejan su trono—¡el Infinito! Que vive—y ama—y salva.

Coronadle Señor del cielo! Uno conocido con el Padre,
Y el Bendito Espíritu, por Él dado desde aquel trono trino de allá!
¡Salve! ¡Redentor—Salve! Porque Tú has muerto por mí;
Tu alabanza nunca, nunca fallará a lo largo de la eternidad.

Coronadle con muchas coronas

—Thring

Coronadle con coronas de oro, todas las naciones grandes y pequeñas,
Coronadle, oh mártires de los antiguos, al Cordero una vez inmolado por todos;
El Cordero una vez inmolado por aquellos que ahora ofrecen sus alabanzas,
Como joyas para la diadema que ciñe su sagrada frente.

Coronadle Hijo de Dios antes de que los mundos comenzaran,
Y vosotros, que pisáis donde Él pisó, coronadle Hijo del hombre;
Que conoció toda aflicción que oprime el pecho humano,
Y las toma y las carga como propias, para que todos en Él puedan descansar.

Coronadle Señor de la luz, que sobre un mundo oscurecido
Con vestidos de gloria infinitos desplegó su ardiente bandera.
Y la llevó en alto, en el cielo—en la tierra—debajo,
Como señal de victoria sobre Satanás, el pecado y la muerte.

Coronadle Señor de la vida que triunfó sobre la tumba,
Y resucitó victorioso en la lucha por aquellos a quienes vino a salvar;
Sus glorias ahora cantamos, Aquel que murió, y resucitó en lo alto.
Que murió para traer vida eterna y vive para que la muerte muera.

Coronadle Señor de señores, que sobre todo reina
Que una vez en la tierra, la Palabra encarnada, por los pecadores redimidos fue inmolada,
Ahora vive en reinos de luz, donde los santos con los ángeles cantan
Sus cánticos delante de Él día y noche, su Dios, Redentor, Rey.

Coronadle Señor del cielo, entronizado en mundos superiores;
Coronadle Rey, a quien se le da el nombre maravilloso de Amor,
Coronadle con muchas coronas, mientras los tronos caen delante de Él.
Coronadle, oh reyes, con muchas coronas, porque Él es Rey de todo.

Matthew Bridges vivió sus últimos años en la provincia de Quebec, Canadá, y luego regresó a Inglaterra antes de su partida de este mundo el 6 de octubre de 1894, a la avanzada edad de 94 años. Aunque no hallamos muchos detalles sobre su vida, nos dejó uno de los himnos más grandes en nuestras manos hoy.

Una gran parte de la perdurabilidad de esta canción es la melodía con la que se la empareja. Este estribillo fue escrito especialmente para esta canción por Sir George Job Elvey en 1868 y recibió el nombre de Diademata. En griego, la palabra diademata significa «una corona real», un nombre apropiado para esta enérgica melodía. El erudito en himnología J. R. Watson está de acuerdo con esto cuando observa: «Diademata constituye un acompañamiento magnífico para el texto, marcial y gozoso sin volverse jamás mecánico o estridente.»

¡Que nuestras congregaciones prosigan la práctica del canto corporativo y con todo el corazón, alzando nuestras voces en alabanza al Señor en la asamblea de los santos! ¡Coronadle, nuestro Señor Jesucristo, con muchas coronas, porque él es digno!

Fuente: A Treasury of Hymn Stories, hymnary.org, umc-discipleship.org, FBC

“O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are His judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? Or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of Him, and through Him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen” (Rom. 11:33–36).

What an exuberant and expressive exclamation written by Apostle Paul! As we look at a new hymn and hymn writer again, let’s keep our minds alert and hearts open to see the hand of God at work.

Matthew Bridges was born at Malden, Essex, in England, on July 14, 1800. He began to publish verses in 1825 and continued until he had published two small volumes of hymns—Hymns of the Heart (1848) and The Passion of Jesus (1852). From here, I will continue with the story by giving a brief history of the church life of our hymnodist.

The hymn writer we are studying in this article was a part of the Anglican Church of England. Around the middle of the 19th century, he became dissatisfied with the church group he was with and found himself following the leading of John Henry Newman in what was called the Oxford Movement. According to hymnologist Albert Bailey, this movement centered on, “Claiming for their Anglican Church lineal descent from the original Apostolic Church.” In pursuit of this, the organization’s followers studied the ancient history of the church, its doctrine, and especially its liturgy. In doing so, they discovered a wealth of Greek and Latin hymnody from the earliest centuries of the Christian church.

As sadly, we find many factions in the Christian church today, so also was the scope of things going on in the mid–1800s. The Oxford Movement seemed in some ways to be a competition between the old and the new way of doing things. In the case of the figure in our story today, it seems he saw a more stable path forward in keeping the old traditions of the mother church, yet he also seemed to have a real, living faith in our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Now, I want to interject here that I trust his decision was made in all good conscience toward God, even though we look on today from an Anabaptist viewpoint and question his reasons for doing so.

We will continue with our story here. Matthew Bridges converted to Roman Catholicism and, wanting to share in the rich hymnic tradition of the Protestant Church, began writing original hymns. Mr. Bridges’ hymns are marked by spirituality and genuine power. One of his hymns we love and enjoy is “Rise, Glorious Conqueror.” Undoubtedly, his greatest hymn is “Crown Him with Many Crowns.” It first appeared in his book The Passion of Jesus, and was originally given the title “The Song of the Seraphs.”

There is an interesting background connected to this hymn, including how there came to be 12 verses. Understandably, only a portion of those verses are being sung today. The selection of verses depends on the hymnal.

Matthew Bridges originally penned the song in 1851. He wrote six stanzas, all based upon Rev. 19:12: “ ... and on His head were many crowns.” The edition by Bridges continued until the 1870s when a devout Anglican clergyman named Godfrey Thring came along. Godfrey was concerned that this popular hymn allowed catholic theology to be sung by protestant congregations. His concerns centered perhaps on Bridges’ original second verse, where he referenced the Blessed Virgin Mary. In light of this, Thring wrote six new stanzas and published it in his Hymns and Sacred Lyrics in 1874.

The 12 stanzas have been mixed and matched down through the years. Interestingly, of the six verses most commonly appearing in hymnals today, three were written by Bridges and three by Thring. The hymn, as published in the Hymns of the Church songbook, completely omits original verse 2 and uses verses 1, 3, 4, part of 5, and part of 6 out of Bridges’ original six verses. The stanzas we sing in that book are highlighted in the selection of verses below. Also included as well are the six couplets by Thring.

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Bridges

Crown Him with many crowns, the Lamb upon His throne;
Hark! how the heavenly anthems drowns all music but its own;
Awake, my soul, and sing of Him who died for thee,
And hail Him as thy matchless King through all eternity.

Crown Him the Virgin’s Son! The God Incarnate born—
Whose arm those crimson trophies won which now His brow adorn!
Fruit of the mystic Rose as of that Rose the Stem:
The Root, whence mercy ever flows—the Babe of Bethlehem!

Crown Him the Lord of peace! Whose power a scepter sways,
From pole to pole, that wars may cease, absorbed in prayer and praise:
His reign shall know no end, and round His pierced feet
Fair flowers of paradise extend their fragrance ever sweet.

Crown Him the Lord of love! Behold His hands and side—
Rich wounds, yet visible above, in beauty glorified:
No angel in the sky can fully bear that sight,
But downward bends his burning eye at mysteries so bright!

Crown Him the Lord of years! The Potentate of time—
Creator of the rolling spheres, ineffably sublime!
Glassed in a sea of light, where everlasting waves
Reflect His throne—the Infinite! Who lives—and loves—and saves.

Crown Him the Lord of heaven! One with the Father known,
And the blest Spirit, through Him given from yonder triune throne!
All hail! Redeemer—Hail! For Thou hast died for me;
Thy praise shall never, never fail throughout eternity!

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Thring

Crown Him with crowns of gold, all nations great and small,
Crown Him, ye martyred saints of old, the Lamb once slain for all;
The Lamb once slain for them who bring their praises now,
As jewels for the diadem that girds His sacred brow.

Crown Him the Son of God before the worlds began,
And ye, who tread where He hath trod, crown Him the Son of man;
Who every grief hath known that wrings the human breast,
And takes and bears them for His own, that all in Him may rest.

Crown Him the Lord of light, Who o’er a darkened world
In robes of glory infinite His fiery flag unfurled.
And bore it raised on high, in heaven—in earth—beneath,
To all the sign of victory o’er Satan, sin, and death.

Crown Him the Lord of life Who triumphed o’er the grave,
And rose victorious in the strife for those He came to save;
His glories now we sing Who died, and rose on high.
Who died, eternal life to bring and lives that death may die.

Crown Him of lords the Lord, Who over all doth reign
Who once on earth, the incarnate Word, for ransomed sinners slain,
Now lives in realms of light, where saints with angels sing
Their songs before Him day and night, their God, Redeemer, King.

Crown Him the Lord of heaven, enthroned in worlds above;
Crown Him the King, to whom is given the wondrous name of Love,
Crown Him with many crowns, as thrones before Him fall.
Crown Him, ye kings, with many crowns, for He is King of all.

Matthew Bridges lived his latter years in the province of Quebec, Canada, then returned to England before his passing from earth on October 6, 1894, at the ripe old age of 94. Although we don’t find many details about his life, he has left one of the greatest hymns in our hands today.

A great part of this song’s enduring quality is the tune it is paired with. This refrain was written especially for this song by Sir George Job Elvey in 1868 and was given the name of Diademata. In Greek, the word diademata means “a royal crown”—a fitting name for this stirring melody. Hymnology scholar J. R. Watson agrees with this when he observes, “Diademata makes a magnificent setting for the text, march-like and joyful without ever becoming mechanical or strident.”

May our congregations continue our practice of corporate, whole-hearted singing, lifting our voices in praise to the Lord in the assembly of the saints! Crown Him, our Lord Jesus Christ, with many crowns, for he is worthy!

“O profondità delle ricchezze sia della sapienza che della conoscenza di Dio! quanto insondabili sono i suoi giudizi e insondabile la sua via! Poiché chi ha conosciuto la mente del Signore? O chi è stato il suo consigliere? O chi gli ha prima dato, e gli sarà ricompensato di nuovo? Poiché di lui, per mezzo di lui e a lui sono tutte le cose: a lui sia la gloria in eterno. Amen” (Rom. 11:33–36).

Che esclamazione esuberante ed espressiva scritta dall'apostolo Paolo! Mentre guardiamo ancora a un nuovo inno e al suo autore, manteniamo la mente vigile e il cuore aperto per vedere la mano di Dio all'opera.

Matthew Bridges nacque a Malden, Essex, in Inghilterra, il 14 luglio 1800. Iniziò a pubblicare versi nel 1825 e continuò fino a pubblicare due piccoli volumi di inni—Hymns of the Heart (1848) e The Passion of Jesus (1852). Da qui, proseguirò la storia dando una breve cronaca della vita ecclesiale del nostro innoautore.

Il compositore di inni che studiamo in questo articolo faceva parte della Chiesa anglicana d'Inghilterra. Intorno alla metà del XIX secolo divenne insoddisfatto del gruppo ecclesiale di cui faceva parte e si trovò a seguire la guida di John Henry Newman in quel che fu chiamato il Movimento di Oxford. Secondo l'imenologo Albert Bailey, questo movimento si centrava sul “reclamare per la loro Chiesa anglicana la discendenza lineare dalla Chiesa apostolica originale.” Nella loro ricerca i seguaci dell'organizzazione studiarono la storia antica della Chiesa, la sua dottrina e soprattutto la sua liturgia. Così scoprirono una ricchezza di inni greci e latini dei primi secoli della Chiesa cristiana.

Come, purtroppo, troviamo oggi molte fazioni nella Chiesa cristiana, così era l'ampiezza delle cose a metà del 1800. Il Movimento di Oxford sembrava in qualche modo una competizione tra il modo antico e quello nuovo di fare le cose. Nel caso della figura della nostra storia odierna, pare che egli vedesse una via più stabile nel mantenere le antiche tradizioni della chiesa madre, eppure sembrava anche avere una fede reale e vivente nel nostro Signore e Salvatore Gesù Cristo. Ora voglio qui interpormi dicendo che confido che la sua decisione sia stata presa a piena coscienza davanti a Dio, anche se noi oggi guardiamo dalla prospettiva anabattista e mettiamo in discussione le sue ragioni.

Proseguiamo con la nostra storia. Matthew Bridges si convertì al cattolicesimo romano e, volendo condividere la ricca tradizione innoica della Chiesa protestante, iniziò a scrivere inni originali. Gli inni di Bridges sono contraddistinti da spiritualità e autentica forza. Uno dei suoi inni che amiamo e apprezziamo è “Rise, Glorious Conqueror.” Indubbiamente, il suo più grande inno è “Crown Him with Many Crowns.” Apparve per la prima volta nel suo libro The Passion of Jesus, e fu originariamente intitolato “The Song of the Seraphs.”

Vi è un interessante retroscena connesso a questo inno, incluso il motivo per cui arrivò ad avere 12 strofe. Comprensibilmente, oggi viene cantata solo una parte di quelle strofe. La selezione delle strofe dipende dall'innario.

Matthew Bridges compose originariamente il canto nel 1851. Scrisse sei strofe, tutte basate su Apoc. 19:12: “ ... e sulla sua testa c'erano molte corone.” L'edizione di Bridges continuò fino agli anni 1870, quando intervenne un devoto chierico anglicano di nome Godfrey Thring. Godfrey era preoccupato che questo popolare inno permettesse che teologia cattolica fosse cantata dalle congregazioni protestanti. Le sue preoccupazioni vertevano forse sulla seconda strofa originale di Bridges, dove faceva riferimento alla Beata Vergine Maria. In considerazione di ciò, Thring scrisse sei nuove strofe e le pubblicò nel suo Hymns and Sacred Lyrics nel 1874.

Le 12 strofe sono state mescolate e abbinate nel corso degli anni. Interessante notare che, delle sei strofe più comunemente presenti negli innari odierni, tre furono scritte da Bridges e tre da Thring. L'inno, così come pubblicato nel songbook Hymns of the Church, omette completamente la strofa originale 2 e usa le strofe 1, 3, 4, parte della 5 e parte della 6 delle sei strofe originali di Bridges. Le strofe che cantiamo in quel libro sono evidenziate nella selezione delle strofe qui sotto. Sono incluse anche le sei terzine di Thring.

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Bridges

Incoronalo di molte corone, l'Agnello sul suo trono;
Ascolta! come gli inni celesti sovrastano ogni musica che non sia la loro;
Svegliati, anima mia, e canta di Colui che morì per te,
E salutalo come tuo Re ineguagliabile per tutta l'eternità.

Incoronalo Figlio della Vergine! Dio incarnato nato—
Il cui braccio quei trofei cremisi guadagnò che ora ornano la sua fronte!
Frutto della Rosa mistica come di quella Rosa il Germoglio:
La Radice, da cui scorre sempre misericordia—il Bambino di Betlemme!

Incoronalo Signore della pace! Il cui potere un suo scettro muove,
Da polo a polo, affinché le guerre cessino, assorbite in preghiera e lode:
Il suo regno non avrà fine, e intorno ai suoi piedi trafitti
I bei fiori del paradiso stendono il loro profumo sempre dolce.

Incoronalo Signore dell'amore! Guarda le sue mani e il suo fianco—
Ferite ricche, eppure visibili in alto, glorificate nella bellezza:
Nessun angelo nel cielo può sopportare pienamente quella vista,
Ma piega il suo occhio ardente in basso dinanzi a misteri tanto splendenti!

Incoronalo Signore degli anni! Il Potentato del tempo—
Creatore delle sfere rotanti, ineffabilmente sublime!
Specchiato in un mare di luce, dove onde eterne
Riflettono il suo trono—l'Infinito! Che vive—e ama—e salva.

Incoronalo Signore del cielo! Uno noto con il Padre,
E lo Spirito benedetto, per mezzo di Lui donato da quel trono trino laggiù!
O gloria al Redentore—Salve! Poiché Tu sei morto per me;
La tua lode non verrà mai, mai meno per tutta l'eternità!

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Thring

Incoronalo con corone d'oro, tutte le nazioni grandi e piccole,
Incoronalo, voi santi martirizzati d'un tempo, l'Agnello una volta immolato per tutti;
L'Agnello una volta immolato per coloro che ora portano le loro lodi,
Come gioielli per il diadema che cinge la sua sacra fronte.

Incoronalo Figlio di Dio prima che i mondi nascessero,
E voi, che calpestate dove Egli ha camminato, incoronatelo Figlio dell'uomo;
Che ha conosciuto ogni afflizione che stringe il petto umano,
E le prende e le porta come proprie, affinché tutti in Lui possano riposare.

Incoronalo Signore della luce, che su un mondo oscurato
Con vesti di gloria infinite spiegò la sua fiammeggiante bandiera.
E la portò alta, in cielo—in terra—sotto,
A tutti segno di vittoria su Satana, peccato e morte.

Incoronalo Signore della vita che trionfò sulla tomba,
E risorse vittorioso nella lotta per coloro che venne a salvare;
Le sue glorie ora cantiamo, Colui che morì e risorse in alto.
Che morì per portare vita eterna e vive affinché la morte muoia.

Incoronalo il Signore dei signori, Colui che su tutti regna
Che una volta sulla terra, la Parola incarnata, per i peccatori riscattati fu ucciso,
Ora vive in regni di luce, dove i santi con gli angeli cantano
Le loro canzoni davanti a Lui giorno e notte, il loro Dio, Redentore, Re.

Incoronalo Signore del cielo, incoronato nei mondi lassù;
Incoronalo il Re, a cui è dato l'ammirevole nome d'Amore,
Incoronalo con molte corone, mentre i troni cadono davanti a Lui.
Incoronatelo, voi re, con molte corone, perché Egli è il Re di tutti.

Matthew Bridges visse gli ultimi anni nella provincia di Québec, in Canada, quindi fece ritorno in Inghilterra prima della sua dipartita il 6 ottobre 1894, alla veneranda età di 94 anni. Sebbene non si trovino molti dettagli sulla sua vita, ci ha lasciato uno dei più grandi inni a nostra disposizione oggi.

Gran parte della qualità duratura di questo canto è dovuta alla melodia con cui è accoppiato. Questo ritornello fu scritto appositamente per il canto da Sir George Job Elvey nel 1868 e fu denominato Diademata. In greco, la parola diademata significa “una corona reale”—un nome adatto per questa melodia vibrante. Lo studioso di inni J. R. Watson concorda osservando, “Diademata fornisce un'imponente cornice al testo, marziale e gioiosa senza mai diventare meccanica o stridente.”

Possa la nostra congregazione proseguire la pratica del canto corale e di tutto il cuore, innalzando le nostre voci in lode al Signore nell'assemblea dei santi! IncoronateLO, il nostro Signore Gesù Cristo, con molte corone, poiché egli è degno!

And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter (John 10:22).

As the maddening winds howl about him, man turns his collar to the cold and damp. Little praise arises for the season that greets him at his weakest point and seeks to discomfort and discourage him from the zest of life. Winter settles in as a formidable authority and arouses anxiety not so much by the infliction of pain but the removal of the pleasant. As we cross the equinox, “the days get longer, and winter gets stronger”, states the old proverb, and it remains incisively correct.

Winter is the season of profound, persistent cold that drives the frost deeper and thickens the ice on the ponds. Man and beast battle its ferocity, and even the lifeless machinery rebels against winter’s adamant arrival. Chilly drafts penetrate every crack and crevice, forcing their heartless presence into the most private chambers. As the woodpiles shrink, utility bills increase in the struggle to resist winter’s array of armed forces. While a few gay tunes, such as Winter Wonderland, seek to capitalize upon its majestic moments, winter is generally despised by the normal inhabitants of this earth. We grimace under the menacing icy grip that holds us captive and longingly anticipate its eventual release.

Spring may have its equal share of soggy and uncomfortable appointments and ragged days. Northern tradition states that the robins must get snowed on three times before the full arrival of spring. But springtime is never void of the hope and glory of better days ahead. Summer can be unbearable with its burning heat and humidity, but it bears a semblance of blessed fruitfulness on every side, and few will slow their activities to notice its discomforts. The autumn days carry their nostalgic enchantment while the beauty of nature is painted in the most remarkable colors on the foliage of the landscape. The bounties of harvest provide an aura of rejoicing in their sheaves, and man’s heart is still merry with the prospects of maturing life. And then comes . . .

Winter

Our Lord experienced the fullness of it; probably not the fullness of the natural elements that those of us in the northern climates face, but the season of apparent fruitlessness. Some said, “He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?” (John 10:20). At a time when there was to be a feast of dedication, “it was winter.” There was a massive division among the people. Confusion reigned on every side. Jesus had just healed a blind man, and the Jews cast him out of the temple. Such fruitless and cold stony hearts inhabited the fields that were acclaimed to be “white unto harvest.” The icy grips of sin had hardened the hearts of humanity, and the meadows of religion were littered with barren stalks draped with the remains of empty husks. The beloved disciple wasted no words when he brought us the fact that . . . it was winter.

“Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter” (Psalm 74:17).

It is easy to believe that God has created summertime. The tunes on a perfect summer day sing to us of the Divine. The beauty revolving about us everywhere speaks of His presence. The cheering birds in every tree, the warmth of the pleasant sunshine, and the amazing prodigy of life draw our hearts to the Giver by a thousand invisible filaments of life. These all testify to the truth that “Thou hast made summer.”

The days of winter are different. “Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46). We share similar sentiments to those of Nathaniel toward the winter months, for it is not so easy to see the hand of God there. There is a great deal of suffering and rejection that we feel penetrating our inner man. I obviously speak not to the season within nature but to the seasons of life that parallel its existence. We do well to aid our frail faith by some solid affirmation that God has made winter, as well, and that we ought not to doubt His divine purposes in it. What, but a season of chilling despair and discomfort can arouse our apathetic souls to . . .

Appreciation

Absence makes the heart grow fonder. Thus does the advent of winter incite our appreciation for summer. We would be blind if summer were perpetually present. It has been aptly said that our dear ones are only ours when we have lost them. When the winter season finally claims their last breath, we then begin to appreciate them for who they really were. It is not the man with an abundance of uninterrupted health who feels most deeply the value of his well-being. That realization arrives on his doorstep the day his health is shattered. There have been many wealthy men who had previously known the stark bareness of bankruptcy. This indelibly embossed a permanent mark in their character that fitted them for the success that followed in its wake.

So the Christian will often experience a season of winter—a time when all that he had labored over, longed for and loved lies languishing beneath the mounds of sterile hopeless drifts. John the Baptist prophesied boldly while the vision was fresh and the crowds pressed around to hear him preach. But the dark and cold prison cell was difficult for him to appreciate. Yet, God has made winter, and these seasons in our lives are paramount to our spiritual well-being.

Strengthening

In the 1700s, a luthier by the name of Stradivari created violins unequaled in their excellence for beautiful sound. As modern experts puzzled long over their inability to create a similar instrument, most have resolved that the wood of the day had been seasoned by difficult winters, producing a quality that cannot be replicated in our day. All nature strains under the duress of the winter months, and man is not exempt. The short days and deep, brazen chill of the night apply a great demand upon our will. In summer, it is comparatively easy to get out of bed at the appointed hour. The earth is warm, the birds are busy singing, and the light is streaming through the open windows. But in the dark of a frigid winter morning, to fling back the covers and arise in a triumphant air is a challenging proposition. It demands a solid resolution to achieve and makes a failure out of many good intentions.

As we broaden that thought to encompass the soul of man, we reach a truth that cannot be denied. Those who have borne the deep burdens of hard living have an innate strength ingrained in their character that those of a mild environment cannot apprehend. The moral character of Adonijah had eroded, for “his father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so?” (1 Kings 1:6). This is the bane of easy living. Those who will insulate themselves on every side from the buffeting of winter will, no doubt, incur a weakening of the will. Those who can conquer their will in the presence of a blatantly cold society are on the highway to success. Summer is languid; but winter makes us resolute. We need to do things even when we don’t feel like doing them. And thus, God has made the winter.

Togetherness

“If two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone?” (Ecc. 4:11). There is no need for such togetherness in the summer—and no desire for it either. The crackling stove has a mesmerizing effect upon the household members and most of our winter evening activities center around it. We speak in the same breath, of hearth and home, and it is in winter that the hearth glows and love grows.

There are but shallow relationships among those who have known no hardship. It takes the heavy austerity of winter to perform the genius of love in our hearts. Adversity levels the playing field, while sage and simpleton pull together in the same yoke. Often, as death wraps its cold fingers around a frail body, loved ones rush to the bedside. Past grievances are forgotten in the solemnity of the moment. It was at the gates of winter that “Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age” (Genesis 25:8). It is here that the separating curtains of the long-standing conflict between Isaac and Ishmael abated and a joint effort between the two brothers “buried him in the cave of Machpelah”.

While none of us shall ever hope for the political unrest that would bring persecution and the removal of religious freedom from our land, it is still my belief that our carnal church divisions will cease upon its advent. It takes winter to pull us together, and Christ was the vehicle upon whom it rode in. “It was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon’s porch” (John 10:23). There, before the inauguration of His death, His disciples were all pushing for the head of the line and striving to be the greatest. Now, after the cold harsh removal of the green tree, they were all found to be “with one accord in Solomon’s porch” (Acts 5:12). Such is the ministry of winter that our God has gifted us with.

Sympathy

For some reason, it seems that we must receive a full dosage of maltreatment before the door of our hearts is unlocked to thoughts of the sorrowful plight of others. One can only wonder what the Good Samaritan must have experienced to be so thoroughly moved by the scene of the man in the ditch. Did not the Jews paint a fresh emblem of hatred and disdain before him on the canvas of each new day? For some, the ill-treatment has a tendency to harden the heart. These go through life in reclusive fashion, with bitterness and spite at the helm of their ship. Any acquaintances that remotely fail their discrimination are categorized as suspect, and avoided.

There are others who have endured the cold blast of winter and loathe that any should have to experience the same. These hearts are quickly aroused to pity and carry bias sympathy toward those of similar plight. Even the rich man who met his wintry death and was now in eternal hell was moved to extend mercy to his five brethren who were bound for the same dreadful destination. How much more should our sluggish hearts stir to charity when met with such discomforts as spiritual winter? Can we greet our fellow man with the same stern, icy glare that has smitten us in the face in bygone days? Is there no storehouse of mercy to extend to the wayward soul who is reaping the cold reality of his folly-filled life that he has sown in his youth?

It was winter in the days when our Lord walked in the temple, and surely, the spiritual environment today is no less frigid. “Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold” (Matthew 24:12). Those of us who choose to despise this barren wilderness can live reclusive at our will. The rest of us shall readily acknowledge that our God hast made . . . winter and allow it to have its perfecting work in our hearts.

예루살렘에 성전 봉헌절이 있을 때라 때는 겨울이었다(요한복음 10:22).

광풍이 그의 주위를 미친 듯이 울부짖을 때, 사람은 옷깃을 세워 찬기와 습기를 막는다. 가장 약한 지점에서 그를 맞이하여 불편하게 하고 삶의 열의를 낙담시키려 하는 계절에 대해 거의 칭찬이 나오지 않는다. 겨울은 강대한 권세로 자리 잡아 서서, 고통을 가함으로라기보다 즐거운 것을 빼앗음으로써 불안을 자아낸다. 분점(춘분·추분)을 지나면서 옛 속담처럼 “날이 길어지고, 겨울은 더 강해진다”는 말이 예리하게 옳다.

겨울은 서릿발을 깊게 하고 연못 위의 얼음을 두껍게 하는 깊고 지속적인 추위의 계절이다. 사람과 짐승은 그 사나움을 견디며, 무생물조차 겨울의 단단한 도래에 반항한다. 차가운 통풍은 모든 틈새로 스며들어 가장 사적인 방까지 무정하게 침투한다. 장작더미가 줄어들수록 공공요금은 늘어나 겨울의 무장한 세력과 맞서 싸우게 된다. Winter Wonderland와 같은 몇몇 경쾌한 곡조들이 그 장엄한 순간을 이용하려 하지만, 겨울은 일반적으로 이 땅의 평범한 거주자들에게 경멸받는다. 우리는 우리를 사로잡는 위협적인 얼음의 손아귀 아래에서 찡그리며 그 끝이 오기를 간절히 기다린다.

봄은 눅눅하고 불편한 약속과 너덜한 날들을 똑같이 안고 있을지 모른다. 북부 전통은 어쩌면 봄이 완전히 도래하기 전에 지빠귀가 세 번 눈을 맞아야 한다고 말한다. 그러나 봄에는 결코 더 좋은 날들에 대한 희망과 영광이 결여되어 있지 않다. 여름은 타는 듯한 더위와 습기로 참기 어렵지만, 사방에 복된 결실의 모습이 보이고 그 불편을 알아채기 위해 활동을 늦추는 사람은 드물다. 가을날은 향수를 불러일으키는 매력이 있고 자연의 아름다움은 풍경의 잎사귀에 가장 놀라운 색채로 칠해진다. 추수의 풍요는 그 단에 기쁨의 기운을 제공하고 사람의 마음은 성숙해지는 삶의 전망으로 여전히 즐겁다. 그리고 그러고 나면 ...

겨울

우리 주님은 그것의 온전함을 경험하셨다; 아마도 북부 기후에 사는 우리들이 직면하는 자연 요소들의 온전함은 아닐지라도 명백한 불모의 계절을 경험하셨다. 어떤 이들은 말하기를 “그는 귀신이 있어 미쳤다; 어찌하여 너희가 그의 말을 들으느냐?”(요한복음 10:20). 봉헌절이 있어야 할 때에 “때는 겨울이었다.” 사람들 사이에는 거대한 분열이 있었다. 모든 면에서 혼란이 지배했다. 예수께서 막 맹인을 고치셨을 때 유대인들은 그를 성전에서 쫓아냈다. ‘추수할 것은 익었도다’라 칭송받던 들판에는 그러한 불수익하고 차가운 돌같은 마음들이 거주하고 있었다. 죄의 얼음 같은 손아귀가 인류의 마음을 단단히 만들었고, 종교의 초원은 빈 껍질의 잔해로 덮인 불모의 대들보들로 흩어져 있었다. 사랑받는 제자는 … 때는 겨울이었다는 사실을 우리에게 전할 때 말을 아끼지 않았다.

“주의가 땅의 모든 경계를 정하셨고 주께서 여름과 겨울을 만드셨나이다”(시편 74:17).

하나님이 여름을 창조하셨다는 것은 쉽게 믿어진다. 완벽한 여름날의 선율은 우리에게 신성을 노래한다. 우리 주위에 도는 아름다움은 그의 임재를 말해 준다. 모든 나무에 지저귀는 새들, 쾌적한 햇빛의 따스함, 그리고 생명의 놀라운 경이로움은 수천의 보이지 않는 생명의 실로 우리 마음을 주께로 끌어당긴다. 이 모든 것은 “주께서 여름을 만드셨다”는 진리를 증언한다.

겨울의 날들은 다르다. “나사렛에서 무슨 선한 것이 날 수 있느냐?”(요한복음 1:46). 우리는 겨울철에 대해 나다나엘의 심정과 비슷한 감정을 공유한다. 그곳에서 하나님의 손을 보는 것은 그리 쉽지 않기 때문이다. 내면을 파고드는 많은 고난과 거절을 느낀다. 나는 분명히 자연 안의 계절이 아니라 그 자연의 존재와 평행을 이루는 삶의 계절들을 말하고 있다. 우리는 하나님이 겨울도 만드셨다는 견고한 확증으로 우리의 연약한 믿음을 돕는 것이 좋다. 무엇이 우리 무관심한 영혼을 일깨우기 위해 빙빙 도는 절망과 불편의 계절보다 더 적절하겠는가 ...

감사

부재는 마음을 더욱 그리워하게 한다. 이와 같이 겨울의 도래는 우리로 하여금 여름을 더 감사하게 만든다. 여름이 영구히 존재했더라면 우리는 눈이 멀었을 것이다. “사랑하는 이들은 잃었을 때에야 비로소 우리 것이 된다”라는 말이 적절하게 적용된다. 겨울이 결국 그들의 마지막 숨을 거두게 할 때, 우리는 그들이 진실로 어떠했는지를 비로소 감사하게 된다. 끊임없는 건강을 가진 사람이 자신의 안녕의 가치를 가장 깊이 느끼는 것은 아니다. 그 깨달음은 그의 건강이 산산조각 나는 날에 문앞에 도착한다. 이전에 파산의 적막한 벌거벗음을 알았던 많은 부유한 사람들이 있었다. 이것은 그들 성격에 지울 수 없는 흔적을 새겨 성공을 위한 자격을 갖추게 했다.

그러므로 그리스도인도 종종 겨울의 계절을 경험할 것이다—그가 수고하고 갈망하며 사랑했던 모든 것이 불모의 눈더미 아래에서 쇠약해져 누워 있는 때. 요한은 비전이 신선하고 무리가 둘러서서 그의 설교를 들을 때 대담하게 예언했다. 그러나 어두운 차가운 감옥 칸은 그에게 이해되기 어려웠다. 그럼에도 하나님은 겨울을 만드셨고, 우리 삶의 이러한 계절들은 우리의 영적 복지에 필수적이다.

강인함

1700년대에 스트라디바리우스라는 명 현악기 제조가는 아름다운 소리에 있어 비할 데 없는 바이올린을 만들었다. 현대의 전문가들이 비슷한 악기를 만드는 데 실패하며 오랫동안 당혹해왔을 때, 대부분은 그 시대의 목재가 어려운 겨울들로 말려들어 오늘날 재현할 수 없는 품질을 만들어 냈다고 결론지었다. 모든 자연은 겨울철의 압박 아래에서 몸부림치며 인간도 예외가 아니다. 짧은 낮과 밤의 깊고 노골적인 한기는 우리의 의지에 큰 요구를 가한다. 여름에는 정해진 시간에 침대에서 나오는 것이 비교적 쉬운 일이다. 대지는 따뜻하고 새들은 노래하느라 바쁘며 빛이 열린 창문으로 쏟아진다. 그러나 얼어붙은 겨울 아침의 어둠 속에서 이불을 젖히고 승리의 기상으로 일어나는 것은 어려운 일이다. 그것은 성취하기 위한 굳은 결단을 요구하며 많은 선한 의도의 실패를 만든다.

그 생각을 인간의 영혼으로 확장하면 부인할 수 없는 진리에 이른다. 고된 삶의 깊은 짐을 견뎌낸 자들은 온화한 환경에서 자란 이들이 이해할 수 없는 타고난 강인함을 성품에 새겨둔다. 아도니야의 도덕적 성품은 침식되었으니 “그의 아비가 때마다 그에게 어찌하여 그렇게 하였느냐고 책망하지 아니하였더라”(열왕기상 1:6). 이것이 안락한 삶의 폐해이다. 사방에서 겨울의 난타를 막아 스스로를 단열하는 자들은 의지의 약화를 면치 못할 것이다. 차갑게 노골적인 사회 앞에서도 자기 의지를 이길 수 있는 자들은 성공으로 가는 길에 서 있다. 여름은 나른하지만 겨울은 우리를 결단력 있게 만든다. 우리는 하고 싶은 마음이 없어도 일을 해야 한다. 그러므로 하나님은 겨울을 만드셨다.

연대

“두 사람이 함께 누우면 서로 따뜻하거니와 한 사람이 어찌하여 따뜻하랴?”(전도서 4:11). 여름에는 이러한 연대의 필요가 없으며 바람도 없다. 탁탁 타는 난로는 가정 구성원들에게 매혹적인 효과를 주며 우리의 겨울 저녁 활동의 대부분은 그것을 중심으로 이루어진다. 우리는 같은 숨결로 난롯불과 가정을 말하며 겨울에 난로는 빛나고 사랑은 자란다.

고난을 모르는 이들 사이에는 천박한 인간관계밖에 없다. 사랑의 천재성을 우리 마음에 실현시키려면 겨울의 엄혹함이 필요하다. 역경은 운동장을 평탄하게 하여 현인과 어리석은 자가 같은 멍에를 메게 한다. 종종 죽음이 연약한 육체에 차가운 손가락을 감쌀 때 사랑하는 이들이 침상으로 달려간다. 그 순간의 엄숙함 속에 과거의 불만은 잊혀진다. “아브라함이 숨을 거두어 노년에 죽었더라”(창세기 25:8). 바로 이곳에서 이삭과 이스마엘 사이의 오랜 갈등의 가르는 장막이 누그러지고 두 형제가 함께 “막벨라 굴에 장사하였더라.”

우리가 정치적 불안으로 박해가 일어나고 종교의 자유가 우리 땅에서 제거되는 일을 바랄 수는 없겠지만, 나의 믿음은 육적인 교회 분열이 겨울의 도래로 멈출 것이라는 점이다. 사람을 하나로 모으는 것은 겨울이며 그 위에 그리스도가 수단이 되어 오셨다. “때는 겨울이라 예수께서 성전 솔로몬 행각에서 다니시니라”(요한복음 10:23). 그곳에서 그의 죽음의 시작 전에 제자들은 모두 선두 자리를 차지하려고 다투며 크게 되려 하였다. 이제 푸른 나무가 냉혹하게 제거된 후, 그들은 모두 “일심으로 솔로몬 행각에 있더라”(사도행전 5:12). 이것이 우리 하나님께서 우리에게 주신 겨울의 사역이다.

동정

어떤 이유에서인지 우리는 마음의 문이 남의 슬픈 처지를 향한 사상으로 열리기 전에 충분한 학대를 받아야만 하는 것 같다. 선한 사마리아인이 도랑에 있는 사람의 광경에 그렇게 철저히 감동을 받았을 때 그가 무슨 일을 겪었는지 궁금하지 않을 수 없다. 유대인들은 매일의 캔버스에 미움과 경멸의 새로운 문장을 그려 놓지 않았는가? 어떤 이들에게는 불공정한 대우가 마음을 단단히 만든다. 이들은 은둔형으로 생을 보내며 쓰라림과 원한을 배의 키로 삼는다. 그들의 판단에 조금이라도 어긋나는 지인은 의심의 범주에 들어 피한다.

다른 이들은 겨울의 차가운 돌풍을 견디고 누구든지 같은 것을 겪어야 한다는 것을 혐오한다. 이 마음들은 곧 연민으로 불타오르며 비슷한 처지의 사람들에게 편애적인 동정을 품는다. 심지어 겨울 같은 죽음을 맞아 지금은 영원한 지옥에 있는 부유한 자도 같은 끔찍한 목적지로 향하는 다섯 형제에게 자비를 베풀어 달라고 간구했다. 영적 겨울과 같은 불편을 마주할 때 우리의 더딘 마음이 자선을 향해 얼마나 더 일어나야 하랴? 과거 우리 얼굴에 들이받았던 그 엄한 얼음 같은 눈초리로 동료를 맞이할 수 있는가? 방황하는 영혼에게 그가 젊은 날에 뿌린 어리석음의 냉혹한 현실을 거두고 있는 자에게 자비의 창고가 전혀 없는가?

주께서 성전 가운데 거니실 때가 겨울이었고 오늘날의 영적 환경도 결코 덜 냉혹하지 않다. “불법이 성하므로 많은 사람의 사랑이 식어지리라”(마태복음 24:12). 이 불모의 광야를 멸시하기로 택한 우리 중 일부는 원하건대 은둔하여 살 수 있다. 나머지 우리들은 우리 하나님이 … 겨울을 만드셨음을 기꺼이 인정하고 그것이 우리 마음 가운데 온전한 일을 하게 허락할 것이다.
