“O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are His judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? Or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of Him, and through Him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen” (Rom. 11:33–36).

What an exuberant and expressive exclamation written by Apostle Paul! As we look at a new hymn and hymn writer again, let’s keep our minds alert and hearts open to see the hand of God at work.

Matthew Bridges was born at Malden, Essex, in England, on July 14, 1800. He began to publish verses in 1825 and continued until he had published two small volumes of hymns—Hymns of the Heart (1848) and The Passion of Jesus (1852). From here, I will continue with the story by giving a brief history of the church life of our hymnodist.

The hymn writer we are studying in this article was a part of the Anglican Church of England. Around the middle of the 19th century, he became dissatisfied with the church group he was with and found himself following the leading of John Henry Newman in what was called the Oxford Movement. According to hymnologist Albert Bailey, this movement centered on, “Claiming for their Anglican Church lineal descent from the original Apostolic Church.” In pursuit of this, the organization’s followers studied the ancient history of the church, its doctrine, and especially its liturgy. In doing so, they discovered a wealth of Greek and Latin hymnody from the earliest centuries of the Christian church.

As sadly, we find many factions in the Christian church today, so also was the scope of things going on in the mid–1800s. The Oxford Movement seemed in some ways to be a competition between the old and the new way of doing things. In the case of the figure in our story today, it seems he saw a more stable path forward in keeping the old traditions of the mother church, yet he also seemed to have a real, living faith in our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Now, I want to interject here that I trust his decision was made in all good conscience toward God, even though we look on today from an Anabaptist viewpoint and question his reasons for doing so.

We will continue with our story here. Matthew Bridges converted to Roman Catholicism and, wanting to share in the rich hymnic tradition of the Protestant Church, began writing original hymns. Mr. Bridges’ hymns are marked by spirituality and genuine power. One of his hymns we love and enjoy is “Rise, Glorious Conqueror.” Undoubtedly, his greatest hymn is “Crown Him with Many Crowns.” It first appeared in his book The Passion of Jesus, and was originally given the title “The Song of the Seraphs.”

There is an interesting background connected to this hymn, including how there came to be 12 verses. Understandably, only a portion of those verses are being sung today. The selection of verses depends on the hymnal.

Matthew Bridges originally penned the song in 1851. He wrote six stanzas, all based upon Rev. 19:12: “ ... and on His head were many crowns.” The edition by Bridges continued until the 1870s when a devout Anglican clergyman named Godfrey Thring came along. Godfrey was concerned that this popular hymn allowed catholic theology to be sung by protestant congregations. His concerns centered perhaps on Bridges’ original second verse, where he referenced the Blessed Virgin Mary. In light of this, Thring wrote six new stanzas and published it in his Hymns and Sacred Lyrics in 1874.

The 12 stanzas have been mixed and matched down through the years. Interestingly, of the six verses most commonly appearing in hymnals today, three were written by Bridges and three by Thring. The hymn, as published in the Hymns of the Church songbook, completely omits original verse 2 and uses verses 1, 3, 4, part of 5, and part of 6 out of Bridges’ original six verses. The stanzas we sing in that book are highlighted in the selection of verses below. Also included as well are the six couplets by Thring.

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Bridges

Crown Him with many crowns, the Lamb upon His throne;
Hark! how the heavenly anthems drowns all music but its own;
Awake, my soul, and sing of Him who died for thee,
And hail Him as thy matchless King through all eternity.

Crown Him the Virgin’s Son! The God Incarnate born—
Whose arm those crimson trophies won which now His brow adorn!
Fruit of the mystic Rose as of that Rose the Stem:
The Root, whence mercy ever flows—the Babe of Bethlehem!

Crown Him the Lord of peace! Whose power a scepter sways,
From pole to pole, that wars may cease, absorbed in prayer and praise:
His reign shall know no end, and round His pierced feet
Fair flowers of paradise extend their fragrance ever sweet.

Crown Him the Lord of love! Behold His hands and side—
Rich wounds, yet visible above, in beauty glorified:
No angel in the sky can fully bear that sight,
But downward bends his burning eye at mysteries so bright!

Crown Him the Lord of years! The Potentate of time—
Creator of the rolling spheres, ineffably sublime!
Glassed in a sea of light, where everlasting waves
Reflect His throne—the Infinite! Who lives—and loves—and saves.

Crown Him the Lord of heaven! One with the Father known,
And the blest Spirit, through Him given from yonder triune throne!
All hail! Redeemer—Hail! For Thou hast died for me;
Thy praise shall never, never fail throughout eternity!

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Thring

Crown Him with crowns of gold, all nations great and small,
Crown Him, ye martyred saints of old, the Lamb once slain for all;
The Lamb once slain for them who bring their praises now,
As jewels for the diadem that girds His sacred brow.

Crown Him the Son of God before the worlds began,
And ye, who tread where He hath trod, crown Him the Son of man;
Who every grief hath known that wrings the human breast,
And takes and bears them for His own, that all in Him may rest.

Crown Him the Lord of light, Who o’er a darkened world
In robes of glory infinite His fiery flag unfurled.
And bore it raised on high, in heaven—in earth—beneath,
To all the sign of victory o’er Satan, sin, and death.

Crown Him the Lord of life Who triumphed o’er the grave,
And rose victorious in the strife for those He came to save;
His glories now we sing Who died, and rose on high.
Who died, eternal life to bring and lives that death may die.

Crown Him of lords the Lord, Who over all doth reign
Who once on earth, the incarnate Word, for ransomed sinners slain,
Now lives in realms of light, where saints with angels sing
Their songs before Him day and night, their God, Redeemer, King.

Crown Him the Lord of heaven, enthroned in worlds above;
Crown Him the King, to whom is given the wondrous name of Love,
Crown Him with many crowns, as thrones before Him fall.
Crown Him, ye kings, with many crowns, for He is King of all.

Matthew Bridges lived his latter years in the province of Quebec, Canada, then returned to England before his passing from earth on October 6, 1894, at the ripe old age of 94. Although we don’t find many details about his life, he has left one of the greatest hymns in our hands today.

A great part of this song’s enduring quality is the tune it is paired with. This refrain was written especially for this song by Sir George Job Elvey in 1868 and was given the name of Diademata. In Greek, the word diademata means “a royal crown”—a fitting name for this stirring melody. Hymnology scholar J. R. Watson agrees with this when he observes, “Diademata makes a magnificent setting for the text, march-like and joyful without ever becoming mechanical or strident.”

May our congregations continue our practice of corporate, whole-hearted singing, lifting our voices in praise to the Lord in the assembly of the saints! Crown Him, our Lord Jesus Christ, with many crowns, for he is worthy!

"Alangkah dalamnya kekayaan, hikmat dan pengetahuan Allah! Sungguh tak terselidiki keputusan-keputusan-Nya dan tak terselami jalan-jalan-Nya! Siapakah yang telah mengetahui pikiran Tuhan, atau siapakah yang menjadi penasehat-Nya? Atau siapakah yang telah lebih dahulu memberi kepada-Nya, sehingga harus dibayar kembali kepadanya? Karena dari Dialah dan oleh Dialah dan kepada Dialah segala sesuatu. Bagi-Nya kemuliaan selama-lamanya. Amin" (Rom. 11:33–36).

Betapa seruan yang meluap dan penuh ekspresi yang ditulis oleh Rasul Paulus! Saat kita melihat kembali pada sebuah himne baru dan penulis himne, marilah kita tetap waspada dan membuka hati untuk melihat tangan Allah yang bekerja.

Matthew Bridges lahir di Malden, Essex, Inggris, pada 14 Juli 1800. Ia mulai menerbitkan bait-bait puisi pada 1825 dan melanjutkannya sampai ia menerbitkan dua buku kecil himne—Hymns of the Heart (1848) dan The Passion of Jesus (1852). Dari sini, saya akan melanjutkan cerita dengan memberikan sejarah singkat tentang kehidupan jemaat dari penulis himne kita.

Penulis himne yang kita pelajari dalam artikel ini adalah bagian dari Gereja Anglikan Inggris. Sekitar pertengahan abad ke-19, ia menjadi tidak puas dengan kelompok gereja tempatnya berada dan mendapati dirinya mengikuti kepemimpinan John Henry Newman dalam apa yang disebut Gerakan Oxford. Menurut ahli hymnologi Albert Bailey, gerakan ini berpusat pada, "Mengklaim bagi Gereja Anglikan mereka keturunan garis lurus dari Gereja Rasul yang asli." Dalam mengejar hal ini, para pengikut organisasi mempelajari sejarah kuno gereja, doktrinnya, dan terutama liturginya. Dalam proses itu, mereka menemukan kekayaan himn-himn Yunani dan Latin dari abad-abad awal gereja Kristen.

Seperti malangnya kita menemukan banyak faksi di gereja Kristen hari ini, demikian pula lingkup kejadian pada pertengahan 1800-an. Gerakan Oxford tampak dalam beberapa hal sebagai persaingan antara cara lama dan cara baru melakukan sesuatu. Dalam kasus sosok dalam cerita kita hari ini, tampaknya ia melihat jalan yang lebih stabil dengan mempertahankan tradisi lama gereja induk, namun ia juga tampak memiliki iman yang nyata dan hidup kepada Tuhan kita dan Juruselamat Yesus Kristus. Kini, saya ingin menyisipkan bahwa saya percaya keputusannya dibuat dengan sepengetahuan hati yang baik di hadapan Allah, walaupun kita melihat sekarang dari sudut pandang Anabaptis dan mempertanyakan alasan-alasannya untuk melakukannya.

Kita akan melanjutkan cerita di sini. Matthew Bridges berpindah ke Katolik Roma dan, ingin berbagi dalam tradisi himne kaya Gereja Protestan, mulai menulis himne asli. Himne-himne Tn. Bridges ditandai oleh spiritualitas dan kekuatan yang tulus. Salah satu himne beliau yang kita cintai dan nikmati adalah "Rise, Glorious Conqueror." Tanpa ragu, himne terbesarnya adalah "Crown Him with Many Crowns." Itu pertama kali muncul dalam bukunya The Passion of Jesus, dan awalnya diberi judul "The Song of the Seraphs."

Ada latar belakang menarik yang terkait dengan himne ini, termasuk bagaimana sampai ada 12 bait. Dapat dimengerti, hanya sebagian bait itu yang dinyanyikan hari ini. Pilihan bait tergantung pada buku nyanyian.

Matthew Bridges awalnya menulis lagu ini pada 1851. Ia menulis enam bait, semuanya berdasarkan Wahyu 19:12: "... dan pada kepalanya terdapat banyak mahkota." Edisi Bridges berlanjut hingga 1870-an ketika seorang rohaniwan Anglikan yang saleh bernama Godfrey Thring muncul. Godfrey khawatir bahwa himne populer ini mengizinkan teologi Katolik dinyanyikan oleh jemaat Protestan. Kekhawatirannya berpusat mungkin pada bait kedua asli Bridges, di mana ia merujuk pada Perawan Maria yang Terberkati. Menyikapi hal itu, Thring menulis enam bait baru dan menerbitkannya dalam Hymns and Sacred Lyrics pada 1874.

Ke-12 bait itu telah dicampur dan dicocokkan sepanjang tahun. Menariknya, dari enam bait yang paling sering muncul dalam buku nyanyian hari ini, tiga ditulis oleh Bridges dan tiga oleh Thring. Himne, sebagaimana diterbitkan dalam buku lagu Hymns of the Church, sepenuhnya menghilangkan bait asli no. 2 dan menggunakan bait 1, 3, 4, bagian dari 5, dan bagian dari 6 dari enam bait asli Bridges. Bait-bait yang kita nyanyikan dalam buku itu disorot dalam pemilihan bait di bawah. Juga disertakan enam pasang bait oleh Thring.

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Bridges

Mahkotailah Dia dengan banyak mahkota, Sang Anak Domba di atas takhtanya;
Dengarlah! bagaimana kidung-kidung sorgawi menenggelamkan segala musik kecuali musiknya sendiri;
Bangkitlah, jiwaku, dan nyanyikan tentang Dia yang mati untukmu,
Dan sambutlah Dia sebagai Rajamu yang tiada tanding sepanjang kekekalan.

Mahkotailah Dia Putra Perawan! Allah yang menjelma lahir—
Di tangan-Nya kemenangan-kemenangan berwarna merah yang kini menghiasi kening-Nya!
Buah dari Mawar mistik sama seperti dari Mawar itu Batangnya:
Akar, tempat kasih karunia selalu mengalir—Bayi dari Betlehem!

Mahkotailah Dia Tuhan damai! Yang kuasa-Nya memegang tongkat kerajaan,
Dari kutub ke kutub, agar peperangan berakhir, larut dalam doa dan pujian:
Pemerintahan-Nya takkan berakhir, dan di sekitar kaki-Nya yang tertikam
Bunga-bunga surga membentangkan harum mereka yang selamanya manis.

Mahkotailah Dia Tuhan kasih! Lihatlah tangan dan lambung-Nya—
Luka-luka berharga, namun tampak di atas, dimuliakan dalam keindahan:
Tak ada malaikat di langit yang dapat sepenuhnya menanggung pemandangan itu,
Tetapi ia menundukkan mata yang menyala pada misteri yang begitu cemerlang!

Mahkotailah Dia Tuhan masa! Yang Berkuasa atas waktu—
Pencipta bola-bola yang berputar, tak terlukiskan kebesaran-Nya!
Tercermin dalam lautan terang, di mana gelombang- gelombang kekal
Memantulkan takhta-Nya—Yang Tak Terbatas! Yang hidup—dan mengasihi—dan menyelamatkan.

Mahkotailah Dia Tuhan sorga! Yang bersatu dikenal dengan Bapa,
Dan Roh yang diberkati, melalui Dia diberikan dari takhta triune di sana!
Salam! Penebus—Salam! Karena Engkau telah mati untukku;
Pujian-Mu takkan pernah, pernah henti sepanjang kekekalan!

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Thring

Mahkotailah Dia dengan mahkota emas, segala bangsa besar dan kecil,
Mahkotailah Dia, hai orang-orang martir zaman dahulu, Sang Anak Domba yang pernah disembelih untuk semua;
Sang Anak Domba yang pernah disembelih bagi mereka yang kini mengangkat pujian mereka,
Sebagai perhiasan untuk diadem yang melingkari kening-Nya yang suci.

Mahkotailah Dia Putra Allah sebelum dunia bermula,
Dan kamu, yang melangkah di mana Dia pernah melangkah, mahkotailah Dia Putra manusia;
Yang telah mengenal tiap duka yang meremukkan dada manusia,
Dan mengambil serta menanggungnya sebagai milik-Nya sendiri, supaya semua dapat beristirahat dalam Dia.

Mahkotailah Dia Tuhan terang, Yang atas dunia yang gelap
Dalam jubah-jubah kemuliaan tanpa batas mengibarkan panji-Nya yang menyala.
Dan mengangkatnya tinggi-tinggi, di sorga—di bumi—di bawah,
Menjadi tanda kemenangan atas Setan, dosa, dan maut.

Mahkotailah Dia Tuhan hidup yang menang atas kubur,
Dan bangkit penuh kemenangan dalam perjuangan bagi mereka yang Ia datangi untuk diselamatkan;
Kini kami menyanyi kemuliaan-Nya yang mati, dan bangkit ke tempat tinggi.
Yang mati, untuk membawa hidup kekal dan hidup yang membuat maut mati.

Mahkotailah Dia Tuhan segala tuan, Yang berkuasa atas segala yang memerintah
Yang dahulu di bumi, Sabda yang menjadi manusia, disalibkan untuk orang berdosa yang ditebus,
Kini hidup di alam cahaya, dimana orang-orang kudus bersama malaikat menyanyi
Nyanyian mereka di hadapan-Nya siang dan malam, Allah mereka, Juruselamat, Raja.

Mahkotailah Dia Tuhan sorga, yang bertakhta di alam di atas;
Mahkotailah Dia Raja, kepada-Nya diberikan nama yang ajaib yaitu Kasih,
Mahkotailah Dia dengan banyak mahkota, saat takhta-takhta roboh di hadapan-Nya.
Mahkotailah Dia, hai raja-raja, dengan banyak mahkota, sebab Ia adalah Raja atas segala.

Matthew Bridges menghabiskan tahun-tahun terakhirnya di provinsi Quebec, Kanada, kemudian kembali ke Inggris sebelum ia meninggalkan dunia pada 6 Oktober 1894, pada usia lanjut 94 tahun. Meskipun kita tidak menemukan banyak rincian tentang hidupnya, ia telah meninggalkan salah satu himne terbesar dalam genggaman kita hari ini.

Bagian besar dari daya tahan lagu ini adalah melodi yang dipadankannya. Refrain ini ditulis khusus untuk lagu ini oleh Sir George Job Elvey pada 1868 dan diberi nama Diademata. Dalam bahasa Yunani, kata diademata berarti "mahkota kerajaan"—sebuah nama yang sesuai untuk melodi yang menggugah ini. Sarjana hymnologi J. R. Watson setuju dengan hal ini ketika ia mengamati, "Diademata membuat pengaturan yang agung bagi teks, seperti lagu mars dan penuh sukacita tanpa pernah menjadi mekanis atau nyaring."

Semoga jemaat-jemaat kita melanjutkan praktik bernyanyi secara bersama dengan sepenuh hati, mengangkat suara kita memuji Tuhan dalam persekutuan orang-orang kudus! Mahkotailah Dia, Tuhan kita Yesus Kristus, dengan banyak mahkota, karena Ia layak!

Sumber: A Treasury of Hymn Stories, hymnary.org, umc-discipleship.org, FBC

A few years ago, I was wallowing in emotional and physical burnout, trying to adjust to life outside of the African village we had called home for eight years. Depression and fear were a regular part of my life. As I slowly crawled out of the hole I was in a hole I never realized I had fallen into until it was too late for an easy remedy, I began to notice beauty.

In those intense years of ministry and language learning in the village, spending time on beauty seemed like a waste of time. And honestly, we lived in a village with very little beauty to offer, the only brightness being the vibrantly colored clothing the women wore. The mud houses, the flat landscape, and dust everywhere were daily life for most months of the year. Though I'm a lover of peace, quiet, and beautiful things, I made very little space in my life for any of it, even the things I could have done in that environment.

We now live in an easier place; the Southern Highlands of Tanzania. Here, there is fresh air and sunshine the whole year long. Flowers... of all kinds, and a lovely house with smooth floors and freshly painted walls. And it's now that I realize how important beauty is to the soul and how important it is to actually notice the beautiful things in my life and create beauty at every possible moment.

Being a mother and homemaker, no matter where in the world God has placed us, is a beautiful thing in itself if we really see it for what it is. It's easy to complain about the daily mundane things that make up my life, the constant dust, or the fact that I'm cooped up in our compound week after week. But I have been surprised with joy. Here are a few things I love to do to keep life fresh and inspiring:

Writing

I especially like to write about the goodness and faithfulness of God. True joy comes from Him, not my circumstances. I’ve believed that for years, but it’s just recently that I’ve actually experienced this reality. My focus is so easily honed in on the things that I wish would be different, thinking that without the uncertainty and difficulties, I’d be happy. I now realize that difficulties have very little to do with the amount of joy found in my heart. Instead, we can allow difficulties to teach us what true joy is and where it comes from.

Keeping a reasonably clean, pleasant house

I try to get rid of the extras and replace the dirty, the dingy, and the ugly with something that is beautiful and lovely. Get rid of the limp, ugly curtain in the schoolroom and replace it with a fresh yellow one (yes, even if it does take a few dollars to do so, I remind my penny-pinching soul).

Clearing off all horizontal surfaces

One of my goals is to clean off all flat surfaces in my house and leave only pleasant, tasteful things. I function so much better if my house is a restful, orderly place. Even though with five children, restful and orderly are relative terms, I’m learning that the rush and mess and noise of a family are beautiful too. It makes the clean floor all the more amazing and thankworthy because it’s a rare experience.

Doing something fun with my children

I like to plan something fun to do with my children, such as a fun science project or an outing. Our favorite is outings to the flower gardens, which are grown here in town along the roadside as a showcase to give other people ideas of how to grow and care for flowers. Tucked into corners here and there, I find all the common flowers I was used to seeing in the States. It’s delightful and even more fun when some of the children share my love for growing things.

Serving food tastefully

Even rice and beans can be served in pretty bowls instead of the messy pots they were cooked in. Raid your local market and you will be surprised with what you can find in glassware and other beautiful dishes that brighten your table.

Speaking cheerfully

Speak cheerfully—to the laundry lady, the house helper, or the neighbor. I can't spend a lot of time in ministry with people other than my children, but there are always people coming around that I can touch with a smile, kindness, or any help they need. It's easy to be peeved over the fact that the produce vendor can't remember NOT to come in the morning while I'm teaching school, and her voice at the door interrupts us again. And what do math facts, bread dough, and dirty floors really have to do with joy? How does the noise of life and cantankerous personalities blend with the eternal? It’s all mixed up in my heart, often with the dusty realities on top and threatening to spill over, but if I give in to peevish attitudes, that is a true joy killer.

Spending time appreciating the beauty of nature

This rests my mind and draws my heart to God. Though I've never lived in the Garden of Eden or places of equal beauty, there's always something to notice, something as small as a patch of green grass struggling to survive the dry season (which is a season of trial for me here in this country). It’s cold (45 degrees or colder in the morning). The green growth and refreshing rains are over. Everything green is dying or has long been dead. Even the house roofs have lost their color as the dust covers every possible surface and threatens to suffocate the inspiration out of humans as well. Even the mountain in view from my kitchen window has lost its beautiful patchwork of gardens and fields. It stands bare and sober, waiting with bated breath for rain—just like my heart. But I’ve delighted in one little patch of earth in our back yard that I keep watered. There are peace lilies, roses, hibiscus, and other bright flowers blooming, and succulents growing in delightful little pots. I lug heavy buckets of water to that spot and sometimes take all five of my children on the city buses to visit yet another flower garden in search of more flowers. It’s not a waste of time for me, as that little spot in my backyard during this dry season refreshes my heart over and over again!

Practicing gratefulness

With a very busy husband, I don’t have a lot of time with him, and he doesn’t have a lot of carefree time with the children. However, I’m making it a habit to notice the small things that do happen, like looking out my kitchen window and seeing him sitting on a mat with the girls, just enjoying them. I stand and watch, thanking God for that moment. It could have gone unnoticed, especially if my heart was full of peevish ungratefulness. Noticing the tiny flashes of joy throughout my day eventually makes my life seem full of joy, though in reality, my life has plenty of trials and challenges.

Life here in town is easier in so many ways, but we’ve been bombarded with many challenges working with the government, which has consumed Tim’s time and energy. Even though we hadn’t lived in the village for over four years, we were doing a lot of support work for our fellow missionaries there and making trips back to where we still felt was our home. But all of us have been banned from that village and have had to work hard to even obtain the necessary documents needed to simply stay in the country.

Recently our compound in the village was taken over by the local army, just weeks after two Tanzanian missionary families moved in. When Tim traveled back to communicate and to hand over the keys out of respect for the ones who were forcing us to do this, he was insulted with hours of irrational anger and mistreatment, along with a lot of demands. Of course, our hearts were broken about seeing our house used for army training rather than for those precious new missionary families who were leaving their homes in town in order to take on the work there.

My husband is exhausted, both physically and emotionally, yet this morning he left for another trip back to the village to “heap on coals of fire” by giving the angry army officer a solar panel and a transformer on top of the other things he demanded. It’s our reasonable service. And yes, my heart had tears in it as I stood at the window and watched him go. I know that he’s only subjecting himself to more mistreatment, and that hurts my heart. But I also know that it’s only through these things that God teaches me joy. As I surrender things dear to my heart, I’m emptied of my own desires. There’s nothing to hang on to anymore and nothing to fight for. So, there’s plenty of room for God to fill my heart with what he wants in there—Joy.

Yes, life hasn’t brought a lot of serendipity my way. There have been a lot of tears, but that’s not my focus anymore, as I purposefully bring beauty into every possible crevice of my life and delight in the surprise of joy. My quest is to allow my home and this tiny space on this earth to be a place where God’s kingdom comes. It can’t be all about happy things, peace, and serendipity, because that isn’t given to me. It’s got to be all about something really good going on in my heart and how that affects everything that my hands touch. My heart can be declaring the works of the Lord as I see him using trials in my life to build my faith and the faith of others looking on. In that way His kingdom comes into this small place, in this little crevice of life, in this space, empty of inspiration, except for His amazing grace, which turns trial into joy.

कुछ साल पहले, मैं भावनात्मक और शारीरिक थकान में डूबी हुई थी, उस अफ्रीकी गाँव से बाहर की ज़िंदगी के अनुकूल होने की कोशिश कर रही थी जिसे हमने आठ साल तक अपना घर कहा था। अवसाद और भय मेरी ज़िंदगी का नियमित हिस्सा थे। जैसे‑जैसे मैं धीरे‑धीरे उस गड्ढे से बाहर रेंगती गई जिसमें मैंने गिरना महसूस ही नहीं किया था जब तक कि आसानी से ठीक होने का समय निकल न गया, मैंने सुंदरता को नोटिस करना शुरू कर दिया।

गाँव में उन तीव्र वर्षों में, जहाँ सेवा और भाषा सीखना था, सुंदरता पर समय बिताना समय की बर्बादी जैसा लगता था। और ईमानदारी से कहूँ तो, हम ऐसे गाँव में रहते थे जहाँ पेश करने के लिए बहुत कम सुंदरता थी, केवल एक उज्जवलता थी महिलाओं के जीवंत रंगीन कपड़ों की। मिट्टी के घर, समतल परिदृश्य, और हर जगह धूल साल के अधिकांश महीनों के लिए दैनिक जीवन थे। हालांकि मैं शांति, सन्नाटा और सुंदर चीजों की प्रेमी हूँ, मैंने अपने जीवन में इन किसी भी चीज़ के लिए बहुत कम जगह बनाई, यहाँ तक कि उन चीज़ों के लिए भी जो मैं उस वातावरण में कर सकती थीं।

अब हम एक आसान जगह में रहते हैं; तंज़ानिया के साउदर्न हाइलैंड्स। यहाँ, पूरे साल ताज़ा हवा और धूप है। फूल... हर तरह के, और एक प्यारा घर जिसमें चिकने फर्श और ताज़ा पेंट किए हुए दीवारें हैं। और अब मुझे एहसास हुआ है कि आत्मा के लिए सुंदरता कितनी महत्वपूर्ण है और यह वास्तव में मेरे जीवन में सुंदर चीजों को नोटिस करना और हर संभव क्षण में सुंदरता बनाना कितना महत्वपूर्ण है।

माँ और गृहिणी होना, चाहे भगवान ने हमें दुनिया में कहीं भी रखा हो, अपने आप में एक सुंदर चीज है अगर हम इसे वास्तव में जैसी है वैसे देखें। मेरे जीवन की रोज़मर्रा की नीरस चीज़ों, लगातार धूल, या इस तथ्य की शिकायत करना कि मैं सप्ताह दर सप्ताह हमारे कंपाउंड में कैद रहती हूँ, आसान है। पर मुझे आनंद की आश्चर्यजनक अनुभूति हुई है। यहाँ कुछ चीजें हैं जो मैं जीवन को ताज़ा और प्रेरणादायक बनाए रखने के लिए करना पसंद करती हूँ:

लिखना

मुझे विशेष रूप से परमेश्वर की भलाई और विश्वासनिष्ठा के बारे में लिखना पसंद है। सच्ची खुशी उनकी है, न कि मेरी परिस्थितियों की। मैंने वर्षों से इसे माना है, लेकिन हाल ही में ही मैंने वास्तव में इस वास्तविकता का अनुभव किया है। मेरा ध्यान इतनी आसानी से उन चीज़ों पर केंद्रित हो जाता है जो मैं चाहती हूँ कि अलग हों, यह सोच कर कि अनिश्चितता और कठिनाइयों के बिना मैं खुश हो जाऊँगी। अब मैं समझती हूँ कि कठिनाइयों का मेरे हृदय में पाई जाने वाली खुशी की मात्रा से बहुत कम लेना‑देना है। इसके बजाय, हम कठिनाइयों को यह सिखाने दे सकते हैं कि सच्ची खुशी क्या है और कहाँ से आती है।

एक तुलनात्मक रूप से साफ़, सुखद घर रखना

मैं अतिरिक्त चीज़ों से छुटकारा पाने की कोशिश करती हूँ और गंदी, फीकी, और बदसूरत चीज़ों की जगह कुछ सुंदर और प्रिय चीज़ रखती हूँ। स्कूलरूम की झुकी‑झुकी, बदसूरत परदे को हटा कर उसे एक ताज़ा पीले परदे से बदल दो (हाँ, भले ही इसके लिए कुछ डॉलर लगें, मैं अपने कट्टर पैसापसंदी आत्मा को याद दिलाती हूँ)।

सभी क्षैतिज सतहों को साफ़ करना

मेरा एक लक्ष्य यह है कि मैं अपने घर की सभी समतल सतहों को साफ़ कर दूँ और केवल सुखद, स्वादपूर्ण चीज़ें छोड़ दूँ। अगर मेरा घर एक विश्रामदायक, सुव्यवस्थित स्थान है तो मुझे काम करने में बहुत बेहतर लगता है। हालांकि पाँच बच्चों के साथ, विश्रामदायक और सुव्यवस्थित सापेक्षक शब्द हैं, मैं सीख रही हूँ कि परिवार की भागदौड़, अव्यवस्था और शोर भी सुंदर होते हैं। यह एक साफ़ फर्श को और भी अद्भुत और धन्यवादयोग्य बनाता है क्योंकि यह एक दुर्लभ अनुभव है।

अपने बच्चों के साथ कुछ मज़ेदार करना

मैं अपने बच्चों के साथ कुछ मज़ेदार योजना बनाना पसंद करती हूँ, जैसे कोई मज़ेदार विज्ञान परियोजना या कोई पिकनिक। हमारा पसंदीदा फूलों के बाग़ों की यात्राएँ हैं, जो यहाँ शहर में सड़क के किनारे उगाए जाते हैं ताकि दूसरे लोगों को यह आईडिया मिल सके कि कैसे फूल उगाएं और उनकी देखभाल करें। यहाँ‑वहाँ छुपे कोनों में, मुझे वे सामान्य फूल मिल जाते हैं जिन्हें मैं अमेरिका में देखने की आदत में थी। यह आनंदित करने वाला है और और भी मज़ेदार तब होता है जब कुछ बच्चे भी मुझसे मिलकर चीज़ें उगाने का प्रेम साझा करते हैं।

खाना स्वादपूर्वक परोसना

यहाँ तक कि चावल और राजमा भी उन गंदे बर्तनों के बजाय सुंदर कटोरियों में परोसे जा सकते हैं जिनमें उन्हें पकाया गया था। अपने स्थानीय बाजार में जाओ और तुम यह देखकर हैरान हो जाओगे कि कांच के बर्तन और अन्य सुंदर बर्तन कितनी सुंदरता से तुम्हारे मेज को रोशन कर सकते हैं।

खुशमिज़ाज़ी से बोलना

खुशमिजाज़ी से बोलो—कपड़ा धोने वाली औरत से, घर की मददगार से, या पड़ोसी से। मैं बच्चों के अलावा ज्यादा लोगों के साथ सेवा में समय नहीं बिता सकती, पर हमेशा लोग आते‑जाते रहते हैं जिन्हें मैं एक मुस्कान, दयालुता, या किसी भी ज़रूरी मदद से छू सकती हूँ। यह आसान है कि मैं चिढ़ जाऊँ इस बात पर कि सब्जी बेचने वाला सुबह के समय याद नहीं रख पाता कि मुझे पढ़ाना है और बार‑बार दरवाज़े पर उसकी आवाज़ हमें विचलित कर देती है। और गणित के तथ्य, आटे का गूँथना, और गंदा फर्श वास्तव में खुशी से क्या लेना‑देना रखते हैं? जीवन की शोर और बड़बोले स्वभाव कैसे अनंत के साथ मिलते हैं? यह सब मेरे हृदय में उलझा हुआ है, अक्सर धूलिल वास्तविकताएँ ऊपर रहती हैं और ओवरफ्लो करने की धमकी देती हैं, पर अगर मैं चिढ़ी प्रवृत्तियों को दांव पर लगाती हूँ, तो वह सच्ची खुशी की हानि है।

प्रकृति की सुंदरता की सराहना में समय बिताना

यह मेरे मन को विश्राम देता है और मेरे हृदय को परमेश्वर की ओर खींचता है। हालाँकि मैंने कभी ईडन का उद्यान या समान सुंदरता वाले स्थानों में नहीं रहा, हमेशा कुछ न कुछ देखने लायक होता है, कुछ इतना छोटा जितना कि सूखे मौसम में जीवित रहने के लिए संघर्ष कर रहा एक हरी घास का टुकड़ा (जो इस देश में मेरे लिए परीक्षा का मौसम है)। सुबह में ठंडा होता है (45 डिग्री या उससे कम)। हरी वृद्धि और ताज़ा बारिश खत्म हो चुकी है। हर हरा मर रहा है या बहुत पहले ही मर चुका है। यहाँ तक कि घरों की छतों ने अपना रंग खो दिया है क्योंकि धूल हर संभव सतह को ढक देती है और मानो इंसानों से प्रेरणा को दम घोंटने की धमकी देती है। यहाँ तक कि मेरी रसोई की खिड़की से दिखने वाला पहाड़ भी अपने बगीचों और खेतों के खूबसूरत पैचवर्क को खो चुका है। वह नग्न और गंभीर खड़ा है, बारिश के लिए सांस रोके प्रतीक्षा कर रहा है—ठीक मेरे हृदय की तरह। पर मैंने हमारे पिछवाड़े की एक छोटी सी जमीन के टुकड़े में आनंद पाया है जिसे मैं पानी देती रहती हूँ। वहाँ पीस लिली, गुलाब, हिबिस्कस, और अन्य चमकीले फूल खिलते हैं, और सुखोपचार पौधे छोटे प्यारे गमलों में बढ़ रहे हैं। मैं भारी बाल्टियाँ पानी के साथ उस स्थान तक ले जाती हूँ और कभी‑कभी अपने सभी पाँच बच्चों को साथ ले कर शहर की बसों पर बैठकर और अधिक फूलों की खोज में किसी और फूलों के बाग़ में ले जाती हूँ। मेरे लिए यह समय की बर्बादी नहीं है, क्योंकि सूखे मौसम में मेरे पिछवाड़े का वह छोटा सा स्थान बार‑बार मेरे हृदय को तरोताजा कर देता है!

कृतज्ञता का अभ्यास करना

एक बहुत व्यस्त पति के साथ, मेरे पास उसके साथ ज्यादा समय नहीं होता, और उसके पास बच्चों के साथ बहुत फुर्सत का समय नहीं होता। हालांकि, मैं यह आदत बना रही हूँ कि उन छोटी‑छोटी चीज़ों को नोटिस करूँ जो होती हैं, जैसे कि रसोई की खिड़की से उसे देखना कि वह गली में चटाई पर बैठा है और लड़कियों के साथ बस आनंद ले रहा है। मैं खड़ी होकर देखती हूँ और उस क्षण के लिए परमेश्वर का धन्यवाद करती हूँ। यह अनदेखा रह सकता था, खासकर अगर मेरा हृदय चिढ़ी अकृतज्ञता से भरा होता। अपने दिन भर में छोटे‑छोटे आनंद के झलकियों को नोटिस करना अंततः मेरी ज़िंदगी को खुशी से भरा हुआ दिखाने लगता है, हालांकि असल में मेरी ज़िंदगी में बहुत सी परीक्षाएँ और चुनौतियाँ हैं।

शहर में यहाँ की ज़िंदगी कई मायनों में आसान है, पर हमें सरकार के साथ काम करने में कई चुनौतियों का सामना करना पड़ा है, जिसने टिम का समय और ऊर्जा खा ली है। हालाँकि हम चार साल से गाँव में नहीं रह रहे थे, हम वहां अपने साथी मिशनरियों के लिए बहुत सारा समर्थन कार्य कर रहे थे और वहाँ हम अभी भी जहाँ हमारा घर महसूस होता था, वहाँ यात्राएँ कर रहे थे। लेकिन हम सभी को उस गाँव से निषिद्ध कर दिया गया है और केवल देश में ठीक‑ठीक रहने के लिए आवश्यक दस्तावेज प्राप्त करने के लिए भी काफ़ी मेहनत करनी पड़ी है।

हाल ही में हमारे कंपाउंड पर स्थानीय सेना ने कब्ज़ा कर लिया, बस कुछ ही हफ्तों बाद जब दो तंज़ानियाई मिशनरी परिवार वहाँ आ बसे थे। जब टिम वापस यात्रा करके संवाद करने और सम्मान के साथ चाबियाँ सौंपने गया उन लोगों को जो हमें ऐसा करने के लिए मजबूर कर रहे थे, तो उसे कई घंटों का तर्कसंगत क्रोध और बुरा बरताव झेलना पड़ा, साथ ही बहुत सी माँगें भी। बेशक, हमारा हृदय टूट गया यह देखकर कि हमारा घर सेना प्रशिक्षण के लिए इस्तेमाल हो रहा है न कि उन कीमती नए मिशनरी परिवारों के लिए जो अपना शहर में घर छोड़कर वहाँ काम संभालने जा रहे थे।

मेरा पति शारीरिक और भावनात्मक दोनों तरह से थका हुआ है, फिर भी आज सुबह वह गाँव वापस एक और यात्रा के लिए निकला ताकि वह उस गुस्सैल सेना अधिकारी को एक सोलर पैनल और एक ट्रांसफॉर्मर दे कर "आग के कोयले ढेर" कर सके, उन अन्य चीज़ों के ऊपर जो उसने मांगी थीं। यह हमारी समझदारी सेवा है। और हाँ, जब मैं खिड़की पर खड़ी होकर उसे जाते देखा तो मेरे हृदय में आँसू थे। मैं जानती हूँ कि वह केवल अपने आप को और अधिक बुरे बर्ताव के हवाले कर रहा है, और यह मेरे हृदय को तकलीफ देता है। पर मैं यह भी जानती हूँ कि केवल इन चीज़ों के द्वारा ही परमेश्वर मुझे खुशी सिखाते हैं। जब मैं अपने प्रिय चीज़ों को समर्पित करती हूँ, तो मैं अपनी इच्छाओं से खाली हो जाती हूँ। अब टिकने के लिए कुछ नहीं बचता और लड़ने के लिए कुछ भी नहीं रह जाता। तो, परमेश्वर के लिए मेरे हृदय को भरने की बहुत जगह बचती है—ख़ुशी।

हाँ, ज़िंदगी ने मेरे लिए बहुत सारी अनपेक्षित शुभवृत्तियाँ नहीं लाईं। बहुत आँसू रहे हैं, पर वह अब मेरा ध्यान नहीं है, क्योंकि मैं जानबूझकर अपने जीवन के हर संभव दरार में सुंदरता लाती हूँ और खुशी के आश्चर्य में आनंद लेती हूँ। मेरा लक्ष्य है कि मेरा घर और इस पृथ्वी पर यह छोटा सा स्थान परमेश्वर का राज्य आए ऐसा जगह बने। यह सब केवल खुशियों, शांति और संयोगों के बारे में नहीं हो सकता, क्योंकि वह सब मुझे नहीं दिया गया। यह मेरे हृदय में चल रही कुछ वास्तव में अच्छी चीज़ों के बारे में होना चाहिए और यह कि यह मेरे हाथों द्वारा छूने वाली हर चीज़ को कैसे प्रभावित करता है। मेरा हृदय प्रभु के कार्यों की घोषणा कर सकता है जैसा कि मैं देखती हूँ कि वह मेरी ज़िंदगी में परीक्षाओं का उपयोग कर मेरी आस्था और देख रहे दूसरों की आस्था का निर्माण कर रहा है। इस तरह उसका राज्य इस छोटे से स्थान में आता है, इस जीवन की छोटी दरार में, इस खाली प्रेरणा की जगह में, सिवाय उसकी अद्भुत कृपा के, जो परीक्षा को खुशी में बदल देती है।

यह लेख अनुरोध पर पुनर्प्रकाशित किया गया है। यह पहली बार The Heartbeat of the Remnant के शरद् 2019 अंक में छपा था। पहले यह Earthen Vessels में छपा था।

A few years ago, I was wallowing in emotional and physical burnout, trying to adjust to life outside of the African village we had called home for eight years. Depression and fear were a regular part of my life. As I slowly crawled out of the hole I was in a hole I never realized I had fallen into until it was too late for an easy remedy, I began to notice beauty.

In those intense years of ministry and language learning in the village, spending time on beauty seemed like a waste of time. And honestly, we lived in a village with very little beauty to offer, the only brightness being the vibrantly colored clothing the women wore. The mud houses, the flat landscape, and dust everywhere were daily life for most months of the year. Though I'm a lover of peace, quiet, and beautiful things, I made very little space in my life for any of it, even the things I could have done in that environment.

We now live in an easier place; the Southern Highlands of Tanzania. Here, there is fresh air and sunshine the whole year long. Flowers... of all kinds, and a lovely house with smooth floors and freshly painted walls. And it's now that I realize how important beauty is to the soul and how important it is to actually notice the beautiful things in my life and create beauty at every possible moment.

Being a mother and homemaker, no matter where in the world God has placed us, is a beautiful thing in itself if we really see it for what it is. It's easy to complain about the daily mundane things that make up my life, the constant dust, or the fact that I'm cooped up in our compound week after week. But I have been surprised with joy. Here are a few things I love to do to keep life fresh and inspiring:

Writing

I especially like to write about the goodness and faithfulness of God. True joy comes from Him, not my circumstances. I’ve believed that for years, but it’s just recently that I’ve actually experienced this reality. My focus is so easily honed in on the things that I wish would be different, thinking that without the uncertainty and difficulties, I’d be happy. I now realize that difficulties have very little to do with the amount of joy found in my heart. Instead, we can allow difficulties to teach us what true joy is and where it comes from.

Keeping a reasonably clean, pleasant house

I try to get rid of the extras and replace the dirty, the dingy, and the ugly with something that is beautiful and lovely. Get rid of the limp, ugly curtain in the schoolroom and replace it with a fresh yellow one (yes, even if it does take a few dollars to do so, I remind my penny-pinching soul).

Clearing off all horizontal surfaces

One of my goals is to clean off all flat surfaces in my house and leave only pleasant, tasteful things. I function so much better if my house is a restful, orderly place. Even though with five children, restful and orderly are relative terms, I’m learning that the rush and mess and noise of a family are beautiful too. It makes the clean floor all the more amazing and thankworthy because it’s a rare experience.

Doing something fun with my children

I like to plan something fun to do with my children, such as a fun science project or an outing. Our favorite is outings to the flower gardens, which are grown here in town along the roadside as a showcase to give other people ideas of how to grow and care for flowers. Tucked into corners here and there, I find all the common flowers I was used to seeing in the States. It’s delightful and even more fun when some of the children share my love for growing things.

Serving food tastefully

Even rice and beans can be served in pretty bowls instead of the messy pots they were cooked in. Raid your local market and you will be surprised with what you can find in glassware and other beautiful dishes that brighten your table.

Speaking cheerfully

Speak cheerfully—to the laundry lady, the house helper, or the neighbor. I can't spend a lot of time in ministry with people other than my children, but there are always people coming around that I can touch with a smile, kindness, or any help they need. It's easy to be peeved over the fact that the produce vendor can't remember NOT to come in the morning while I'm teaching school, and her voice at the door interrupts us again. And what do math facts, bread dough, and dirty floors really have to do with joy? How does the noise of life and cantankerous personalities blend with the eternal? It’s all mixed up in my heart, often with the dusty realities on top and threatening to spill over, but if I give in to peevish attitudes, that is a true joy killer.

Spending time appreciating the beauty of nature

This rests my mind and draws my heart to God. Though I've never lived in the Garden of Eden or places of equal beauty, there's always something to notice, something as small as a patch of green grass struggling to survive the dry season (which is a season of trial for me here in this country). It’s cold (45 degrees or colder in the morning). The green growth and refreshing rains are over. Everything green is dying or has long been dead. Even the house roofs have lost their color as the dust covers every possible surface and threatens to suffocate the inspiration out of humans as well. Even the mountain in view from my kitchen window has lost its beautiful patchwork of gardens and fields. It stands bare and sober, waiting with bated breath for rain—just like my heart. But I’ve delighted in one little patch of earth in our back yard that I keep watered. There are peace lilies, roses, hibiscus, and other bright flowers blooming, and succulents growing in delightful little pots. I lug heavy buckets of water to that spot and sometimes take all five of my children on the city buses to visit yet another flower garden in search of more flowers. It’s not a waste of time for me, as that little spot in my backyard during this dry season refreshes my heart over and over again!

Practicing gratefulness

With a very busy husband, I don’t have a lot of time with him, and he doesn’t have a lot of carefree time with the children. However, I’m making it a habit to notice the small things that do happen, like looking out my kitchen window and seeing him sitting on a mat with the girls, just enjoying them. I stand and watch, thanking God for that moment. It could have gone unnoticed, especially if my heart was full of peevish ungratefulness. Noticing the tiny flashes of joy throughout my day eventually makes my life seem full of joy, though in reality, my life has plenty of trials and challenges.

Life here in town is easier in so many ways, but we’ve been bombarded with many challenges working with the government, which has consumed Tim’s time and energy. Even though we hadn’t lived in the village for over four years, we were doing a lot of support work for our fellow missionaries there and making trips back to where we still felt was our home. But all of us have been banned from that village and have had to work hard to even obtain the necessary documents needed to simply stay in the country.

Recently our compound in the village was taken over by the local army, just weeks after two Tanzanian missionary families moved in. When Tim traveled back to communicate and to hand over the keys out of respect for the ones who were forcing us to do this, he was insulted with hours of irrational anger and mistreatment, along with a lot of demands. Of course, our hearts were broken about seeing our house used for army training rather than for those precious new missionary families who were leaving their homes in town in order to take on the work there.

My husband is exhausted, both physically and emotionally, yet this morning he left for another trip back to the village to “heap on coals of fire” by giving the angry army officer a solar panel and a transformer on top of the other things he demanded. It’s our reasonable service. And yes, my heart had tears in it as I stood at the window and watched him go. I know that he’s only subjecting himself to more mistreatment, and that hurts my heart. But I also know that it’s only through these things that God teaches me joy. As I surrender things dear to my heart, I’m emptied of my own desires. There’s nothing to hang on to anymore and nothing to fight for. So, there’s plenty of room for God to fill my heart with what he wants in there—Joy.

Yes, life hasn’t brought a lot of serendipity my way. There have been a lot of tears, but that’s not my focus anymore, as I purposefully bring beauty into every possible crevice of my life and delight in the surprise of joy. My quest is to allow my home and this tiny space on this earth to be a place where God’s kingdom comes. It can’t be all about happy things, peace, and serendipity, because that isn’t given to me. It’s got to be all about something really good going on in my heart and how that affects everything that my hands touch. My heart can be declaring the works of the Lord as I see him using trials in my life to build my faith and the faith of others looking on. In that way His kingdom comes into this small place, in this little crevice of life, in this space, empty of inspiration, except for His amazing grace, which turns trial into joy.

’n Paar jaar gelede het ek in emosionele en fisieke uitbranding gesukkel en probeer aanpas by die lewe buite die Afrika-dorpie wat vir agt jaar ons tuiste was. Depressie en vrees was ’n gereelde deel van my lewe. Terwyl ek stadig uit die put gekruip het waarin ek was — ’n put waarvan ek nooit regtig besef het dat ek daarin geval het totdat dit te laat was vir ’n maklike geneesmiddel nie — het ek begin die skoonheid opmerk.

In daardie intense jare van bediening en taalleer in die dorpie het dit soos ’n vermorsing van tyd gelyk om tyd aan skoonheid te gee. En eerlik gesê, ons het in ’n dorpie gewoon wat baie min skoonheid aangebied het, die enigste helderheid was die lewendige klere wat die vroue gedra het. Die modderhuise, die plat landskap en stof oral was die daaglikse lewe vir die meeste maande van die jaar. Al is ek ’n liefhebber van vrede, stilte en pragtige dinge, het ek baie min plek in my lewe daarvoor gemaak, selfs die dinge wat ek in daardie omgewing kon doen.

Ons woon nou op ’n makliker plek; die Suidelike Hooglande van Tanzanië. Hier is vars lug en sonskyn die hele jaar deur. Blomme... van alle soorte, en ’n lieflike huis met gladde vloere en vars geskilderde mure. En dit is nou dat ek besef hoe belangrik skoonheid vir die siel is en hoe belangrik dit is om werklik die pragtige dinge in my lewe te sien en skoonheid by elke moontlike geleentheid te skep.

Om ’n moeder en huishoudster te wees, waar ook al God ons geplaas het, is op sigself ’n pragtige ding as ons dit regtig sien soos dit is. Dit is maklik om te kla oor die daaglikse alledaagse dinge wat my lewe uitmaak, die konstante stof, of die feit dat ek week na week in ons erf opgesluit is. Maar ek is verras met vreugde. Hier is ’n paar dinge wat ek graag doen om die lewe vars en inspirerend te hou:

Skryf

Ek hou veral daarvan om te skryf oor die goedheid en getrouheid van God. Ware vreugde kom van Hom, nie van my omstandighede nie. Ek het dit al jare geglo, maar dit is eers onlangs dat ek hierdie werklikheid regtig ervaar het. My fokus word so maklik gefokus op die dinge wat ek wens anders was, gedinkend dat sonder onsekerheid en moeilikhede ek gelukkig sou wees. Ek besef nou dat moeilikhede baie min te doen het met die hoeveelheid vreugde in my hart. In plaas daarvan kan ons moeilikhede toelaat om ons te leer wat ware vreugde is en waar dit vandaan kom.

Om die huis redelik skoon en behaaglik te hou

Ek probeer om die oortolliges uit te gooi en die vuil, die flou en die lelike te vervang met iets wat mooi en bekoorlik is. Gooi die slappe, lelike gordyn in die skoolkamer uit en vervang dit met ’n vars geel een (ja, selfs al kos dit ’n paar dollars om te doen, herinner ek my stuursugtige siel daaraan).

Alle horisontale oppervlaktes opruim

Een van my doelwitte is om alle plat oppervlaktes in my huis skoon te maak en slegs aangename, smaakvolle dinge te laat staan. Ek funksioneer soveel beter as my huis ’n rustige, ordelike plek is. Al beteken rustigheid en orde iets anders met vyf kinders, leer ek dat die gejaag, rommel en geraas van ’n gesin ook pragtig is. Dit maak die skoon vloer nog meer wonderlik en dankbaar omdat dit ’n seldsame ervaring is.

Iets pret saam met my kinders doen

Ek hou daarvan om iets pret te beplan om saam met my kinders te doen, soos ’n prettige wetenskapprojek of ’n uitstappie. Ons gunsteling is uitstappies na die blomtuiste, wat hier in die dorp langs die pad aangeplant word as ’n vertoonplek om ander mense idees te gee oor hoe om blomme te kweek en te versorg. In klein hoekies hier en daar vind ek al die gewone blomme waaraan ek in die VSA gewoond was. Dit is heerlik en nog meer pret wanneer sommige van die kinders my liefde vir plantgoed deel.

Etense smaakvol bedien

Selfs rys en bone kan in pragtige bakke bedien word in plaas van in die morsige potte waarin dit gekook is. Raai jou plaaslike mark, en jy sal verbaas wees oor wat jy in glasware en ander pragtige skottelgoed kan vind wat jou tafel ophelder.

Volksvriendelik praat

Praat vrolik—met die wassersvrou, die huiswerker of die buurvrou. Ek kan nie baie tyd in bediening met ander mense spandeer behalwe my kinders nie, maar daar is altyd mense wat rondkom wat ek met ’n glimlag, vriendelikheid of enige hulp wat hulle nodig het, kan raak. Dis maklik om kwaad te wees oor die feit dat die groenteverkoper nie kan onthou om nie in die oggend te kom terwyl ek skool gee nie, en haar stem by die deur ons weer onderbreek. En wat het syferfeite, brooddeeg en vuil vloere eintlik met vreugde te doen? Hoe meng die geraas van die lewe en hese persoonlikhede met die ewigheid? Dit is alles deurmekaar in my hart, dikwels met die stofrealiteite bo-op wat dreig om oor te loop, maar as ek aan kwaai gesindhede toegee, is dit ’n ware vreugde-doder.

Tyd spandeer om die skoonheid van die natuur te waardeer

Dit rus my gedagtes en trek my hart na God. Al het ek nog nooit in die Tuin van Eden of plekke van gelyke skoonheid gewoon nie, is daar altyd iets om op te let, iets so klein soos ’n plekkie groen gras wat sukkel om die droë seisoen te oorleef (wat hier in hierdie land ’n seisoen van beproewing vir my is). Dit is koud (45 grade of kouer in die oggend). Die groen groei en verfrissende reën is verby. Alles wat groen is sterf of is lankal dood. Selfs die dakke van huise het hul kleur verloor soos die stof elke moontlike oppervlak bedek en dreig om die inspirasie uit mense te versmoor ook. Selfs die berg wat vanuit my kombuiskamer se venster sigbaar is, het sy pragtige lapwerk van tuine en lande verloor. Dit staan kaal en ernstig en wag met ingehoue asem vir reën—net soos my hart. Maar ek het vreugde gevind in een klein plekkie grond in ons agterplaas wat ek nat hou. Daar is vredelelieë, rose, hibiskus en ander helder blomme wat blom, en vetplante wat in lieflike potte groei. Ek sleep swaar emmers water na daardie plek en neem soms al vyf my kinders op die stadsbusse om nog ’n blomtuiste te besoek op soek na meer blomme. Vir my is dit geen vermorsing van tyd nie, want daardie klein plekkie in my agterplaas tydens hierdie droë seisoen verfris my hart oor en oor!

Dankbaarheid beoefen

Met ’n baie besige man het ek nie baie tyd met hom nie, en hy het nie baie sorgelose tyd saam met die kinders nie. Tog maak ek dit ’n gewoonte om die klein dinge wat gebeur, op te let, soos om uit my kombuisvenster te kyk en hom op ’n mat saam met die dogters te sien sit, net hulle geniet. Ek staan en kyk en dank God vir daardie oomblik. Dit kon ongemerk verbygegaan het, veral as my hart vol kleinzielige ondankbaarheid was. Om die klein flitse van vreugde deur my dag op te let, laat uiteindelik my lewe vol vreugde lyk, alhoewel daar in werklikheid baie beproewings en uitdagings in my lewe is.

Die lewe hier in die dorp is op soveel maniere makliker, maar ons is gebombardeer met baie uitdagings in ons werk met die regering, wat Tim se tyd en energie opgeslurp het. Al het ons nie vir meer as vier jaar in die dorpie gewoon nie, het ons baie ondersteuningswerk vir ons mede-missionarisse daar gedoen en terugreise gemaak na waar ons steeds gevoel het dit is ons huis. Maar ons almal is uit daardie dorpie verban en moes hard werk om selfs die nodige dokumente te bekom wat benodig is om eenvoudig in die land te bly.

Onlangs is ons kamp in die dorpie net weke nadat twee Tanzaniese sendingsgesinne ingetrek het, deur die plaaslike weermag oorneem. Toe Tim terugreis om te kommunikeer en uit respek vir diegene wat ons daartoe gedwing het, die sleutels oor te gee, is hy beledig met ure van irrasionele woede en mishandeling, saam met baie eise. Ons harte was natuurlik gebreek om te sien dat ons huis deur die weermag vir opleiding gebruik is in plaas van vir daardie kosbare nuwe sendingsgesinne wat hul huise in die dorp verlaat het om die werk daar aan te pak.

My man is uitgeput, beide fisies en emosioneel, tog het hy vanoggend weer vertrek vir nog ’n reis terug na die dorpie om die woedende offisier "kole van vuur op te hoop" deur ’n sonpaneel en ’n transformator bo-op die ander goedere wat hy geëis het, te gee. Dit is ons redelike diens. En ja, my hart het gehuil toe ek by die venster gestaan en hom sien gaan. Ek weet dat hy homself net aan nóg meer mishandeling onderwerp, en dit maak my hart seer. Maar ek weet ook dat dit net deur hierdie dinge is dat God my vreugde leer. Terwyl ek dinge wat my dierbaar is oorgee, raak ek leeg van my eie begeertes. Daar is niks meer om aan vas te hou nie en niks meer om vir te baklei nie. Dus is daar ruim plek vir God om my hart te vul met wat Hy daarin wil hê—Vreugde.

Ja, die lewe het nie baie serendipiteit na my toe gebring nie. Daar was baie trane, maar dit is nie meer my fokus nie, want ek bring doelbewus skoonheid in elke moontlike skeur van my lewe en geniet die verrassing van vreugde. My strewe is om my huis en hierdie klein plekkie op aarde ’n plek te laat wees waar God se koninkryk kom. Dit kan nie alles oor blydskap, vrede en geluk toeval wees nie, want dit word my nie toegeneem nie. Dit moet alles gaan oor iets werklik goed wat in my hart gebeur en hoe dit alles wat my hande raak, beïnvloed. My hart kan die werke van die Here verklaar terwyl ek hom sien gebruik maak van beproewings in my lewe om my geloof en die geloof van ander wat toekyk te bou. Op daardie manier kom Sy koninkryk in hierdie klein plek, in hierdie klein skeur van die lewe, in hierdie ruimte, leeg van inspirasie, behalwe Sy wonderlike genade, wat beproewing in vreugde omskep.

The article is reprinted by request. It was first printed in The Heartbeat of the Remnant in the Autumn 2019 issue. Previously printed in Earthen Vessels.

“O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are His judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? Or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of Him, and through Him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen” (Rom. 11:33–36).

What an exuberant and expressive exclamation written by Apostle Paul! As we look at a new hymn and hymn writer again, let’s keep our minds alert and hearts open to see the hand of God at work.

Matthew Bridges was born at Malden, Essex, in England, on July 14, 1800. He began to publish verses in 1825 and continued until he had published two small volumes of hymns—Hymns of the Heart (1848) and The Passion of Jesus (1852). From here, I will continue with the story by giving a brief history of the church life of our hymnodist.

The hymn writer we are studying in this article was a part of the Anglican Church of England. Around the middle of the 19th century, he became dissatisfied with the church group he was with and found himself following the leading of John Henry Newman in what was called the Oxford Movement. According to hymnologist Albert Bailey, this movement centered on, “Claiming for their Anglican Church lineal descent from the original Apostolic Church.” In pursuit of this, the organization’s followers studied the ancient history of the church, its doctrine, and especially its liturgy. In doing so, they discovered a wealth of Greek and Latin hymnody from the earliest centuries of the Christian church.

As sadly, we find many factions in the Christian church today, so also was the scope of things going on in the mid–1800s. The Oxford Movement seemed in some ways to be a competition between the old and the new way of doing things. In the case of the figure in our story today, it seems he saw a more stable path forward in keeping the old traditions of the mother church, yet he also seemed to have a real, living faith in our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Now, I want to interject here that I trust his decision was made in all good conscience toward God, even though we look on today from an Anabaptist viewpoint and question his reasons for doing so.

We will continue with our story here. Matthew Bridges converted to Roman Catholicism and, wanting to share in the rich hymnic tradition of the Protestant Church, began writing original hymns. Mr. Bridges’ hymns are marked by spirituality and genuine power. One of his hymns we love and enjoy is “Rise, Glorious Conqueror.” Undoubtedly, his greatest hymn is “Crown Him with Many Crowns.” It first appeared in his book The Passion of Jesus, and was originally given the title “The Song of the Seraphs.”

There is an interesting background connected to this hymn, including how there came to be 12 verses. Understandably, only a portion of those verses are being sung today. The selection of verses depends on the hymnal.

Matthew Bridges originally penned the song in 1851. He wrote six stanzas, all based upon Rev. 19:12: “ ... and on His head were many crowns.” The edition by Bridges continued until the 1870s when a devout Anglican clergyman named Godfrey Thring came along. Godfrey was concerned that this popular hymn allowed catholic theology to be sung by protestant congregations. His concerns centered perhaps on Bridges’ original second verse, where he referenced the Blessed Virgin Mary. In light of this, Thring wrote six new stanzas and published it in his Hymns and Sacred Lyrics in 1874.

The 12 stanzas have been mixed and matched down through the years. Interestingly, of the six verses most commonly appearing in hymnals today, three were written by Bridges and three by Thring. The hymn, as published in the Hymns of the Church songbook, completely omits original verse 2 and uses verses 1, 3, 4, part of 5, and part of 6 out of Bridges’ original six verses. The stanzas we sing in that book are highlighted in the selection of verses below. Also included as well are the six couplets by Thring.

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Bridges

Crown Him with many crowns, the Lamb upon His throne;
Hark! how the heavenly anthems drowns all music but its own;
Awake, my soul, and sing of Him who died for thee,
And hail Him as thy matchless King through all eternity.

Crown Him the Virgin’s Son! The God Incarnate born—
Whose arm those crimson trophies won which now His brow adorn!
Fruit of the mystic Rose as of that Rose the Stem:
The Root, whence mercy ever flows—the Babe of Bethlehem!

Crown Him the Lord of peace! Whose power a scepter sways,
From pole to pole, that wars may cease, absorbed in prayer and praise:
His reign shall know no end, and round His pierced feet
Fair flowers of paradise extend their fragrance ever sweet.

Crown Him the Lord of love! Behold His hands and side—
Rich wounds, yet visible above, in beauty glorified:
No angel in the sky can fully bear that sight,
But downward bends his burning eye at mysteries so bright!

Crown Him the Lord of years! The Potentate of time—
Creator of the rolling spheres, ineffably sublime!
Glassed in a sea of light, where everlasting waves
Reflect His throne—the Infinite! Who lives—and loves—and saves.

Crown Him the Lord of heaven! One with the Father known,
And the blest Spirit, through Him given from yonder triune throne!
All hail! Redeemer—Hail! For Thou hast died for me;
Thy praise shall never, never fail throughout eternity!

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Thring

Crown Him with crowns of gold, all nations great and small,
Crown Him, ye martyred saints of old, the Lamb once slain for all;
The Lamb once slain for them who bring their praises now,
As jewels for the diadem that girds His sacred brow.

Crown Him the Son of God before the worlds began,
And ye, who tread where He hath trod, crown Him the Son of man;
Who every grief hath known that wrings the human breast,
And takes and bears them for His own, that all in Him may rest.

Crown Him the Lord of light, Who o’er a darkened world
In robes of glory infinite His fiery flag unfurled.
And bore it raised on high, in heaven—in earth—beneath,
To all the sign of victory o’er Satan, sin, and death.

Crown Him the Lord of life Who triumphed o’er the grave,
And rose victorious in the strife for those He came to save;
His glories now we sing Who died, and rose on high.
Who died, eternal life to bring and lives that death may die.

Crown Him of lords the Lord, Who over all doth reign
Who once on earth, the incarnate Word, for ransomed sinners slain,
Now lives in realms of light, where saints with angels sing
Their songs before Him day and night, their God, Redeemer, King.

Crown Him the Lord of heaven, enthroned in worlds above;
Crown Him the King, to whom is given the wondrous name of Love,
Crown Him with many crowns, as thrones before Him fall.
Crown Him, ye kings, with many crowns, for He is King of all.

Matthew Bridges lived his latter years in the province of Quebec, Canada, then returned to England before his passing from earth on October 6, 1894, at the ripe old age of 94. Although we don’t find many details about his life, he has left one of the greatest hymns in our hands today.

A great part of this song’s enduring quality is the tune it is paired with. This refrain was written especially for this song by Sir George Job Elvey in 1868 and was given the name of Diademata. In Greek, the word diademata means “a royal crown”—a fitting name for this stirring melody. Hymnology scholar J. R. Watson agrees with this when he observes, “Diademata makes a magnificent setting for the text, march-like and joyful without ever becoming mechanical or strident.”

May our congregations continue our practice of corporate, whole-hearted singing, lifting our voices in praise to the Lord in the assembly of the saints! Crown Him, our Lord Jesus Christ, with many crowns, for he is worthy!

Sourced from: A Treasury of Hymn Stories, hymnary.org, umc-discipleship.org, FBC

« Ô profondeur des richesses, de la sagesse et de la connaissance de Dieu ! Que ses jugements sont insondables et impénétrables ses voies ! Car qui a connu la pensée du Seigneur ? Qui l'a été son conseiller ? Qui lui a donné premièrement, et cela lui sera rendu ? Car de lui, par lui et pour lui sont toutes choses. À lui la gloire aux siècles ! Amen » (Rom. 11:33–36).

Quelle exclamation exubérante et expressive écrite par l’apôtre Paul ! En regardant à nouveau un nouvel hymne et un nouvel auteur d'hymnes, gardons notre esprit vigilant et notre cœur ouvert pour voir la main de Dieu à l’œuvre.

Matthew Bridges est né à Malden, dans l'Essex, en Angleterre, le 14 juillet 1800. Il commença à publier des vers en 1825 et continua jusqu'à avoir fait paraître deux petits volumes d'hymnes—Hymns of the Heart (1848) et The Passion of Jesus (1852). À partir d'ici, je poursuivrai l'histoire en donnant un bref historique de la vie ecclésiale de notre hymnodiste.

Le parolier étudié dans cet article faisait partie de l'Église anglicane d'Angleterre. Vers le milieu du XIXe siècle, il devint mécontent du groupe ecclésial auquel il appartenait et se trouva à suivre la direction de John Henry Newman dans ce qu'on appela le Mouvement d'Oxford. Selon l'hymnologue Albert Bailey, ce mouvement se centra sur « revendiquer pour leur Église anglicane une descendance linéaire de l'Église apostolique originelle ». Dans cette quête, les partisans de l'organisation étudièrent l'histoire ancienne de l'Église, sa doctrine et surtout sa liturgie. Ce faisant, ils découvrirent une richesse d'hymnodie grecque et latine provenant des premiers siècles de l'Église chrétienne.

Aussi tristement que nous trouvons de nombreuses factions dans l'Église chrétienne aujourd'hui, il en était de même au milieu des années 1800. Le Mouvement d'Oxford sembla en certains points être une compétition entre l'ancien et le nouveau mode d'agir. Dans le cas de la figure de notre récit, il semble qu'il ait vu une voie plus stable en conservant les anciennes traditions de l'Église-mère, et pourtant il semblait aussi posséder une foi réelle et vivante en notre Seigneur et Sauveur Jésus-Christ. Je veux insérer ici que je fais confiance au fait que sa décision fut prise en toute bonne conscience devant Dieu, même si nous regardons aujourd'hui depuis un point de vue anabaptiste et remettons en question ses raisons de le faire.

Nous poursuivrons notre récit ici. Matthew Bridges se convertit au catholicisme romain et, désirant partager la riche tradition hymnologique de l'Église protestante, commença à écrire des hymnes originaux. Les hymnes de M. Bridges se distinguent par leur spiritualité et leur puissance authentique. L'un de ses hymnes que nous aimons et dont nous jouissons est « Rise, Glorious Conqueror ». Sans aucun doute, son plus grand hymne est « Crown Him with Many Crowns ». Il apparut pour la première fois dans son livre The Passion of Jesus, et fut à l'origine intitulé « The Song of the Seraphs ».

Il y a un arrière‑plan intéressant lié à cet hymne, y compris la manière dont il en est venu à compter 12 couplets. Il est compréhensible que seule une partie de ces couplets soit chantée aujourd'hui. Le choix des couplets dépend de l'hymnaire.

Matthew Bridges rédigea initialement le chant en 1851. Il écrivit six strophes, toutes fondées sur Apoc. 19:12 : « ... et sur sa tête il y avait plusieurs diadèmes. » L'édition de Bridges continua jusqu'aux années 1870 lorsqu'un ecclésiastique anglican dévot nommé Godfrey Thring intervint. Godfrey craignait que cet hymne populaire permettait à une théologie catholique d'être chantée par des congrégations protestantes. Ses préoccupations portaient peut‑être sur le deuxième couplet original de Bridges, où il faisait référence à la Bienheureuse Vierge Marie. En conséquence, Thring écrivit six nouvelles strophes et les publia dans son Hymns and Sacred Lyrics en 1874.

Les 12 strophes ont été mélangées et assorties au fil des années. Fait intéressant, des six couplets apparaissant le plus souvent dans les hymnaires aujourd'hui, trois furent écrits par Bridges et trois par Thring. L'hymne, tel que publié dans le recueil Hymns of the Church, omet complètement le couplet original 2 et utilise les couplets 1, 3, 4, une partie du 5 et une partie du 6 des six couplets originaux de Bridges. Les strophes que nous chantons dans ce livre sont mises en évidence dans la sélection de vers ci‑dessous. Sont également incluses les six strophes de Thring.

Couronnez‑le de nombreuses couronnes

—Bridges

Couronnez‑le de nombreuses couronnes, l’Agneau sur son trône ;
Écoute ! comme les cantiques célestes couvrent toute musique qui n’est pas la leur ;
Réveille‑toi, mon âme, et chante celui qui est mort pour toi,
Et salue‑le comme ton Roi incomparable à travers l’éternité.

Couronnez‑le, le Fils de la Vierge ! Le Dieu incarné né—
Dont le bras remporta ces trophées cramoisis qui ornent maintenant son front !
Fruit de la Rose mystique comme de cette Rose la Tige :
La Racine, d’où la miséricorde coule sans cesse—l’Enfant de Bethléem !

Couronnez‑le, le Seigneur de la paix ! Dont le pouvoir brandit un sceptre,
D’un pôle à l’autre, pour que les guerres cessent, absorbées en prière et en louange :
Son règne ne connaîtra pas de fin, et autour de ses pieds percés
De magnifiques fleurs du paradis étendent leur parfum toujours doux.

Couronnez‑le, le Seigneur de l’amour ! Voici ses mains et son côté—
Riches blessures, pourtant visibles au‑dessus, glorifiées dans la beauté :
Aucun ange dans le ciel ne peut supporter pleinement ce spectacle,
Mais il incline son regard ardent vers le bas devant des mystères si brillants !

Couronnez‑le, le Seigneur des âges ! Le Potentat du temps—
Créateur des sphères tournantes, ineffablement sublime !
Miroité dans une mer de lumière, où des vagues éternelles
Reflètent son trône—l’Infini ! Qui vit—et aime—et sauve.

Couronnez‑le, le Seigneur du ciel ! Un avec le Père connu,
Et l’Esprit béni, donné par lui depuis ce trône trinitaire là‑bas !
Salut, Rédempteur—Salut ! Car tu es mort pour moi ;
Ta louange ne faillira jamais, jamais à travers l’éternité !

Couronnez‑le de nombreuses couronnes

—Thring

Couronnez‑le de couronnes d’or, toutes les nations grandes et petites,
Couronnez‑le, ô saints martyrisés d’autrefois, l’Agneau jadis immolé pour tous ;
L’Agneau jadis immolé pour ceux qui apportent maintenant leurs louanges,
Comme des joyaux pour le diadème qui ceint son front sacré.

Couronnez‑le, le Fils de Dieu avant que les mondes ne commencent,
Et vous, qui marchez là où il a marché, couronnez‑le le Fils de l’homme ;
Qui a connu toute affliction qui serre la poitrine humaine,
Et les prend et les porte pour lui‑même, afin que tous reposent en lui.

Couronnez‑le, le Seigneur de la lumière, qui sur un monde obscurci
Dans des robes de gloire infinie déploya son drapeau ardent.
Et le porta élevé, au ciel—sur la terre—en dessous,
Pour tous le signe de la victoire sur Satan, le péché et la mort.

Couronnez‑le, le Seigneur de la vie, qui triompha de la tombe,
Et ressuscita victorieux dans la lutte pour ceux qu’il vint sauver ;
Ses gloires maintenant nous chantons, lui qui mourut et s’éleva haut.
Qui mourut, pour apporter la vie éternelle et vit pour que la mort puisse mourir.

Couronnez‑le, Seigneur des seigneurs, qui règne sur tous
Qui jadis sur la terre, le Verbe incarné, fut pour des pécheurs rachetés immolé,
Vit maintenant dans des royaumes de lumière, où les saints chantent avec les anges
Leurs chants devant lui jour et nuit, leur Dieu, Rédempteur, Roi.

Couronnez‑le, le Seigneur des cieux, trôné dans des mondes d’en haut ;
Couronnez‑le, le Roi, à qui est donné le nom merveilleux d’Amour,
Couronnez‑le de nombreuses couronnes, tandis que les trônes tombent devant lui.
Couronnez‑le, ô rois, de nombreuses couronnes, car il est le Roi de tous.

Matthew Bridges vécut ses dernières années dans la province de Québec, au Canada, puis retourna en Angleterre avant de quitter ce monde le 6 octobre 1894, à l’âge avancé de 94 ans. Bien que nous ne trouvions pas beaucoup de détails sur sa vie, il nous a laissé l’un des plus grands hymnes dont nous disposons aujourd’hui.

Une grande part de la qualité durable de ce chant tient à la mélodie qui l’accompagne. Ce refrain fut spécialement composé pour ce chant par Sir George Job Elvey en 1868 et porta le nom de Diademata. En grec, le mot diademata signifie « une couronne royale »—un nom approprié pour cette mélodie entraînante. L'hymnologue J. R. Watson est d'accord avec cela lorsqu'il observe : « Diademata constitue une mise en musique magnifique pour le texte, martiale et joyeuse sans jamais devenir mécanique ou stridente. »

Puisse nos congrégations poursuivre la pratique du chant communautaire, avec tout leur cœur, élevant nos voix en louange au Seigneur dans l’assemblée des saints ! Couronnez‑le, notre Seigneur Jésus‑Christ, de nombreuses couronnes, car il est digne !

Source : A Treasury of Hymn Stories, hymnary.org, umc-discipleship.org, FBC

The people we commonly refer to as the Russian Mennonites came into being as a group in a way quite similar to that of us with an Anabaptist heritage. We sprang from the same areas of Europe, from much of the same teachings of early Anabaptism, and have both experienced many of the same temptations and pitfalls, though at different times and locations.

This article will not focus on the beginnings of the Russian Mennonites apart from a brief overview. The group first entered Russia upon the urgings of the Viceroy Potemkin, who came into authority over the area now known as Ukraine after its annexation by Russia in 1783. The area had been under his partial administration since 1774, and he was eager to populate the land with foreign settlers. The residents of New Russia, as it was then called, were mostly nomads and Cossacks, a seminomadic group present in the steppes of Russia. The Mennonites in Danzig, Poland, were first approached with the offer of land, which would have appealed to them because they were routinely denied land ownership as a semi-persecuted people at that time. This offer came in August of 1786, and two brothers from the Danzig church were sent to survey the land and make arrangements for possible immigration.

The first immigration of 462 families began in 1788, and the “Old Colony” was established at Chortitza. They were afforded freedom of religion, exemption from military service, and the right to maintain their own schools and governances.

The Mennonites thrived in their new homeland. Although the first years were hard, partially due to the fact that mostly poorer families and those not in church leadership chose to resettle in Russia, the group soon began to transform the barren plains and steppes into rich agricultural communities. As the churches grew, so did their prosperity.

This period of relative peace lasted for over a century, until the late 1800s, when the Russian government, dissatisfied with the number of foreign settlements inside its borders, began applying pressure to many of the groups it had invited to settle its land some 100 years before. The Mennonites were not the only ones targeted, as many groups from various nations had established themselves in Russia. Steps taken against the Mennonites included pressure to participate in the armed forces as well as pressure to drop the German language that the communities had been using in favor of the Russian language. As these pressures increased, some Mennonites chose to flee the country in the 1870s. The majority, however, by now quite wealthy and affluent in comparison to their Russian peasant neighbors, chose to stay and weather the storm.

Unbeknownst to them, a full-scale revolution that would reshape Russia as a country was just around the corner. In 1917, the Bolsheviks came to power through the October Revolution, an event where the reigning tsar, or emperor, was deposed and exiled, and a new government was set up. A civil war broke out, and much of the fighting raged over the lands occupied by the Mennonites. Here, it is necessary to insert a brief history of the ideology of this new government.

The October Revolution and its subsequent change in government were fueled by a class war. As opposed to Nazi Germany, where a person could be arrested and killed for their race, in Russia, a person could and would be arrested for their class, for example, property ownership was seen as a crime against the people, and so the wealthier class of Russian peasants and farmers, those who most often owned property and employed the lower class of peasants, became an instant target a revolution that claimed to want to distribute all property and resources evenly amongst its citizenry.

By this time, the strong agricultural society of the Mennonites had transformed Ukraine into a breadbasket, its vast fields sown with wheat developed specifically by the Mennonites: Turkey Red Wheat. This hardy crop had made the Mennonite church quite wealthy, and their colonies had grown and flourished into villages of comfort and, at times, extravagance. This must have been a two-fold insult to the still impoverished peasants of Russia. Not only was there a large group of people in their midst that taught, spoke, and did their dealings in a language not of the Motherland, but these people also were wealthy beyond most peasants’ dreams.

It is, therefore, no surprise that when the kulaks, the wealthy class of peasants, came under persecution from the new government, the Mennonites were seen as the enemy of the people. As the civil war raged over Mennonite lands, villages were burnt and decimated, people executed or driven off, and livestock and grain plundered. Eventually, this period of fighting did come to an end, but for those few who survived the destruction, there was no reprieve to be found.

With the label of kulak and being generally defenseless, the Mennonites faced intense persecution. Religious services were rarely allowed, and the agricultural communities that had fed Russia and many others besides were collectivized and put under government control. Many of their churches ceased to exist entirely, although those in the east tended to last longer than the western villages.

Imagine then, to a people accustomed for generations to the favor and benevolence of material possessions and success, that all things material are stripped away. In a historical eye blink, the wealthy become the poor, and the favored become the hated. Even with a strong Christian faith, such a turn of events would shock and confuse.

But further tests were yet ahead for those who endured the first 25 years of the Soviet persecution. With the memory of their easy lives still fresh, the dawn of World War II brought a unique and enticing opportunity: the rise of a government that promoted the well-being of the German race, that valued those groups that could turn an empty prairie into a sprawling farm, that was vehemently anti-Communist- to this beleaguered group of believers, this must have seemed to be a God sent miracle to deliver them from their burdensome exile.

And so, they embraced the invading Germans. We readers, who are blessed with the ability to see the end result of these people’s decisions, can certainly make a good guess at what the end result was of wholesale support for the Nazis, but we must remember the scenarios that these Mennonites found themselves in...it was not one that would have been easy to decipher and decide upon if it were to be judged by man’s knowledge.

And so it was that the descendants of those helpless believers who gave their bodies at the stake and sword aligned themselves with a worldly kingdom that promised to protect and provide for them. In exchange for an eternal heritage, they chose to hope that the might of the German army would win back their earthly heritage and riches, and it was in this might that they trusted, forming bands of men who fought alongside the Germans against their old neighbors.

History did not deviate from its course, and the German army was eventually beaten back to its own borders and then further, and yet further into German lands. Before this retreating army ran those that had looked to it for their deliverance.

The atrocities of the Soviet government against its citizens are well documented in various works, most famously in the Gulag Archipelago, a book written by a Russian officer who was accused of treason. That author, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, painted a terrible picture of the treatment and exile of those who had opposed the USSR. Amongst the imprisoned or executed millions described in his tomes, there lie the remnants of a people who began as we did, experienced the smile of prosperity as we do, and then, treasuring that prosperity, lost it in calamitous fashion. We would do well to consider the paths we choose, as the wise king of the Scriptures instructs us, lest we, too, fall in the pursuit of prosperity. “Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established” (Proverbs 4:26).
