Дирк оглядывал зал, пытаясь быть незаметным, но совершенно неудачно крутился и вертелся на своём месте. Он хотел найти брата Сайласa до начала службы. Каждое воскресное утро он вытягивал шею в поисках седой головы самого старого члена общины, и каждый раз его мать бросала на Дирка тот взгляд, который означал: «Сиди спокойно и смотри вперёд».

В это утро ему даже не пришлось смотреть назад. В двух рядах от сцены Дирк заметил белые волосы брата Сайласа и его чёрный жилет. Для Дирка этот жилет был очень особенным. В кармане того жилета было нечто очень важное. В том кармане лежали мятные конфеты. Конфетки Lifesavers, если быть точным. И всё, что должен был сделать маленький мальчик, чтобы получить одну из этих конфет, — подойти к брату Сайласу после службы и вежливо попросить. И тогда брат Сайлас улыбался, опускал руку в внутренний карман, вынимал конфету и вручал её мальчику.

Именно поэтому Дирк так тщательно искал по церковному дому, где находится брат Сайлас, — чтобы знать, куда идти за той самой мятой. Это воскресенье не отличалось от других, и как только было произнесено последнее «Аминь», рой мальчиков и девочек начал сгущаться вокруг брата Сайласа, как синицы у кормушки. Брат Сайлас любезно раздавал свои конфеты по очереди, всё ещё продолжая беседовать с мужчинами. Когда настал черёд Дирка, он добросовестно сказал: «Спасибо», даже не подумав, что именно произнёс.

Дирк не стал медлить с поеданием этой мятной конфеты, и прежде чем он успел опомниться, конфета была съедена, и он мог продолжать свой день и остаток недели.

В четверг зазвонил телефон, и когда его мать подняла трубку, Дирк понял, что это записанное сообщение, потому что мать слушала, не вступая в разговор. Он особо не задумывался об этом, до тех пор пока позже вечером не подслушал, как родители обсуждают это сообщение.

«В какой больнице сказали, что находится брат Сайлас? Сказали ли, как долго он там пробудет? Может, нам стоит навестить его», — сказала мать.

«Я думаю, нам стоит навестить его», — ответил отец.

«Он будет в церкви в воскресенье?» — вмешался Дирк, остановив движение своего трактора, чтобы услышать ответ.

«Нет, думаю, пройдёт довольно много времени, прежде чем он почувствует себя достаточно хорошо, чтобы прийти в церковь. Он очень болен, Дирк», — сказал отец. Ни отец, ни мать не ожидали той реакции, которую вызвал этот ответ. Дирк начал плакать, и сначала они были тронуты, что он так сочувствует брату Сайласу. А затем Дирк начал капризничать.

«А как же моя конфета? Если брата Сайласа не будет в церкви, я не получу свою конфету! Он просто обязан быть в церкви!» Он мог бы продолжать так бесконечно, если бы родители его не остановили.

«Дирк Филлипс, во‑первых, мы не ходим на церковные службы для того, чтобы ты получил конфету. Мы ходим на службы, чтобы поклоняться Богу. Кроме того, тебе следует беспокоиться о брате Сайласе, а не о том, получишь ли ты конфету. Как бы ты себя чувствовал, если бы твои друзья заботились только о том, что ты им даёшь, и не интересовались, как у тебя дела?» — «Прости. Я так не думал», — всхлипнул Дирк, вытирая нос рукавом.

«Можешь ли ты вспомнить кого‑нибудь в Библии, кто жаловался, когда не получал того, чего хотел?» — спросила мать. Дирку никто не приходил в голову, хотя он был уверен, что в Библии таких примеров предостаточно. «Израильтяне, Дирк. Они часто жаловались, и это не угождало Богу», — подсказала она.

Тогда отец попросил Дирка прочитать Числа 11 и переписать те места, которые показывают неблагодарность и как Бог относился к ней. Родители заверили Дирка, что подумают о визите к брату Сайласу. Они предложили по пути заехать в магазин и взять пакет мятных конфет специально для брата Сайласа.

Когда настал день визита к брату Сайласу, отец взял сына в магазин, чтобы выбрать пакет мятных конфет. «Ты когда‑нибудь задумывался, сколько раз брату Сайласу приходится делать это, чтобы карманы у него были полны конфет для всех вас, детей?» — спросил он Дирка, у которого глаза расширились от этого небольшого откровения.

«Нет, я об этом не думал. Но, наверное, ему приходилось покупать целый пакет каждую неделю! Нас в церкви много детей.»

Прошёл целый месяц, прежде чем брат Сайлас почувствовал себя достаточно хорошо, чтобы снова ходить в церковь. Когда это случилось, глаза Дирка загорелись при виде его. В конце службы Дирк сначала задержался, прежде чем подойти. Честно говоря, ему было немного стыдно. Но, наблюдая, как другие дети получают свои конфеты и видя непременный блеск в глазах брата Сайласа, когда он их раздаёт, Дирк почувствовал себя увереннее. Он тоже присоединился к толпе.

«Я рад, что вы поправились, брат Сайлас. Мне не хватало вас», — прошептал Дирк, глядя в лицо доброго господина.

«И я рад! Очень приятно вернуться. Я тоже соскучился по этому месту», — ответил брат Сайлас, мягко положив руку на плечо Дирка во время разговора. Затем он опустил руку в карман жилета и вынул конфету. Конфету Lifesaver, если быть точным. И на этот раз, когда Дирк произнёс «спасибо», это было уже с чувством благодарности, а не только словами.

And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter (John 10:22).

As the maddening winds howl about him, man turns his collar to the cold and damp. Little praise arises for the season that greets him at his weakest point and seeks to discomfort and discourage him from the zest of life. Winter settles in as a formidable authority and arouses anxiety not so much by the infliction of pain but the removal of the pleasant. As we cross the equinox, “the days get longer, and winter gets stronger”, states the old proverb, and it remains incisively correct.

Winter is the season of profound, persistent cold that drives the frost deeper and thickens the ice on the ponds. Man and beast battle its ferocity, and even the lifeless machinery rebels against winter’s adamant arrival. Chilly drafts penetrate every crack and crevice, forcing their heartless presence into the most private chambers. As the woodpiles shrink, utility bills increase in the struggle to resist winter’s array of armed forces. While a few gay tunes, such as Winter Wonderland, seek to capitalize upon its majestic moments, winter is generally despised by the normal inhabitants of this earth. We grimace under the menacing icy grip that holds us captive and longingly anticipate its eventual release.

Spring may have its equal share of soggy and uncomfortable appointments and ragged days. Northern tradition states that the robins must get snowed on three times before the full arrival of spring. But springtime is never void of the hope and glory of better days ahead. Summer can be unbearable with its burning heat and humidity, but it bears a semblance of blessed fruitfulness on every side, and few will slow their activities to notice its discomforts. The autumn days carry their nostalgic enchantment while the beauty of nature is painted in the most remarkable colors on the foliage of the landscape. The bounties of harvest provide an aura of rejoicing in their sheaves, and man’s heart is still merry with the prospects of maturing life. And then comes . . .

Winter

Our Lord experienced the fullness of it; probably not the fullness of the natural elements that those of us in the northern climates face, but the season of apparent fruitlessness. Some said, “He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?” (John 10:20). At a time when there was to be a feast of dedication, “it was winter.” There was a massive division among the people. Confusion reigned on every side. Jesus had just healed a blind man, and the Jews cast him out of the temple. Such fruitless and cold stony hearts inhabited the fields that were acclaimed to be “white unto harvest.” The icy grips of sin had hardened the hearts of humanity, and the meadows of religion were littered with barren stalks draped with the remains of empty husks. The beloved disciple wasted no words when he brought us the fact that . . . it was winter.

“Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter” (Psalm 74:17).

It is easy to believe that God has created summertime. The tunes on a perfect summer day sing to us of the Divine. The beauty revolving about us everywhere speaks of His presence. The cheering birds in every tree, the warmth of the pleasant sunshine, and the amazing prodigy of life draw our hearts to the Giver by a thousand invisible filaments of life. These all testify to the truth that “Thou hast made summer.”

The days of winter are different. “Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46). We share similar sentiments to those of Nathaniel toward the winter months, for it is not so easy to see the hand of God there. There is a great deal of suffering and rejection that we feel penetrating our inner man. I obviously speak not to the season within nature but to the seasons of life that parallel its existence. We do well to aid our frail faith by some solid affirmation that God has made winter, as well, and that we ought not to doubt His divine purposes in it. What, but a season of chilling despair and discomfort can arouse our apathetic souls to . . .

Appreciation

Absence makes the heart grow fonder. Thus does the advent of winter incite our appreciation for summer. We would be blind if summer were perpetually present. It has been aptly said that our dear ones are only ours when we have lost them. When the winter season finally claims their last breath, we then begin to appreciate them for who they really were. It is not the man with an abundance of uninterrupted health who feels most deeply the value of his well-being. That realization arrives on his doorstep the day his health is shattered. There have been many wealthy men who had previously known the stark bareness of bankruptcy. This indelibly embossed a permanent mark in their character that fitted them for the success that followed in its wake.

So the Christian will often experience a season of winter—a time when all that he had labored over, longed for and loved lies languishing beneath the mounds of sterile hopeless drifts. John the Baptist prophesied boldly while the vision was fresh and the crowds pressed around to hear him preach. But the dark and cold prison cell was difficult for him to appreciate. Yet, God has made winter, and these seasons in our lives are paramount to our spiritual well-being.

Strengthening

In the 1700s, a luthier by the name of Stradivari created violins unequaled in their excellence for beautiful sound. As modern experts puzzled long over their inability to create a similar instrument, most have resolved that the wood of the day had been seasoned by difficult winters, producing a quality that cannot be replicated in our day. All nature strains under the duress of the winter months, and man is not exempt. The short days and deep, brazen chill of the night apply a great demand upon our will. In summer, it is comparatively easy to get out of bed at the appointed hour. The earth is warm, the birds are busy singing, and the light is streaming through the open windows. But in the dark of a frigid winter morning, to fling back the covers and arise in a triumphant air is a challenging proposition. It demands a solid resolution to achieve and makes a failure out of many good intentions.

As we broaden that thought to encompass the soul of man, we reach a truth that cannot be denied. Those who have borne the deep burdens of hard living have an innate strength ingrained in their character that those of a mild environment cannot apprehend. The moral character of Adonijah had eroded, for “his father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so?” (1 Kings 1:6). This is the bane of easy living. Those who will insulate themselves on every side from the buffeting of winter will, no doubt, incur a weakening of the will. Those who can conquer their will in the presence of a blatantly cold society are on the highway to success. Summer is languid; but winter makes us resolute. We need to do things even when we don’t feel like doing them. And thus, God has made the winter.

Togetherness

“If two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone?” (Ecc. 4:11). There is no need for such togetherness in the summer—and no desire for it either. The crackling stove has a mesmerizing effect upon the household members and most of our winter evening activities center around it. We speak in the same breath, of hearth and home, and it is in winter that the hearth glows and love grows.

There are but shallow relationships among those who have known no hardship. It takes the heavy austerity of winter to perform the genius of love in our hearts. Adversity levels the playing field, while sage and simpleton pull together in the same yoke. Often, as death wraps its cold fingers around a frail body, loved ones rush to the bedside. Past grievances are forgotten in the solemnity of the moment. It was at the gates of winter that “Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age” (Genesis 25:8). It is here that the separating curtains of the long-standing conflict between Isaac and Ishmael abated and a joint effort between the two brothers “buried him in the cave of Machpelah”.

While none of us shall ever hope for the political unrest that would bring persecution and the removal of religious freedom from our land, it is still my belief that our carnal church divisions will cease upon its advent. It takes winter to pull us together, and Christ was the vehicle upon whom it rode in. “It was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon’s porch” (John 10:23). There, before the inauguration of His death, His disciples were all pushing for the head of the line and striving to be the greatest. Now, after the cold harsh removal of the green tree, they were all found to be “with one accord in Solomon’s porch” (Acts 5:12). Such is the ministry of winter that our God has gifted us with.

Sympathy

For some reason, it seems that we must receive a full dosage of maltreatment before the door of our hearts is unlocked to thoughts of the sorrowful plight of others. One can only wonder what the Good Samaritan must have experienced to be so thoroughly moved by the scene of the man in the ditch. Did not the Jews paint a fresh emblem of hatred and disdain before him on the canvas of each new day? For some, the ill-treatment has a tendency to harden the heart. These go through life in reclusive fashion, with bitterness and spite at the helm of their ship. Any acquaintances that remotely fail their discrimination are categorized as suspect, and avoided.

There are others who have endured the cold blast of winter and loathe that any should have to experience the same. These hearts are quickly aroused to pity and carry bias sympathy toward those of similar plight. Even the rich man who met his wintry death and was now in eternal hell was moved to extend mercy to his five brethren who were bound for the same dreadful destination. How much more should our sluggish hearts stir to charity when met with such discomforts as spiritual winter? Can we greet our fellow man with the same stern, icy glare that has smitten us in the face in bygone days? Is there no storehouse of mercy to extend to the wayward soul who is reaping the cold reality of his folly-filled life that he has sown in his youth?

It was winter in the days when our Lord walked in the temple, and surely, the spiritual environment today is no less frigid. “Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold” (Matthew 24:12). Those of us who choose to despise this barren wilderness can live reclusive at our will. The rest of us shall readily acknowledge that our God hast made . . . winter and allow it to have its perfecting work in our hearts.

En dit was te Jerusalem die fees van die toewyding, en dit was winter (Johannes 10:22).

Terwyl die woeste winde om hom huil, trek die mens sy kraag styf teen die koue en vogtigheid. Min lof word uitgespreek vir die seisoen wat hom op sy swakste punt ontmoet en hom probeer ontstel en ontmoedig van die lewenslus. Winter kom neer as ŉ formidabele gesag en wek angs nie soveel deur die toediening van pyn nie, maar deur die wegneming van die aangename. Soos ons die equinox oorsteek, stel die ou spreekwoord dat “die dae langer word, en die winter sterker raak”, en dit bly skerp korrek.

Winter is die seisoen van diep, volgehoue koue wat die ryp dieper dryf en die ys op die damme verdik. Mens en dier baklei teen sy felheid, en selfs die lewelose masjinerie verzet hom teen die harde koms van die winter. Koue trek deur elke krake en skuiwholte en dwing hul hartelose teenwoordigheid in die intiemste vertrekke. Soos die houtstapels krimp, styg die nutsrekeninge in die stryd om weerstand te bied teen die winter se gevegsmagte. Terwyl enkele vrolike deuntjies, soos Winter Wonderland, probeer baat by sy majesteitlike oomblikke, word winter oor die algemeen deur die gewone inwoners van hierdie aarde versmaad. Ons maak gesigte onder die dreigende ysgryp wat ons gevangen hou en verlang na sy uiteindelike vrystelling.

Lente mag haar deel soggende en ongemaklike dae hê en geskeurde oomblikke. Noordelike tradisie sê dat die swartebosvinke drie keer in die sneeu moet beland voordat die lente volkome aankom. Maar lentyd is nooit sonder die hoop en heerlikheid van beter dae wat voorlê nie. Somer kan ondraaglik wees met sy brandende hitte en humiditeit, maar dit dra ’n skynbare seën van vrugbaarheid aan elke kant, en min sal hul aktiwiteite vertraag om sy ongemak te opmerk. Die herfsdae dra hul nostalgiese bekoring terwyl die skoonheid van die natuur in die merkwaardigste kleure op die blare van die landskap geskilder word. Die oorvloed van die oes skep ŉ atmosfeer van vreugde in hul skofte, en die mens se hart bly vrolik oor die vooruitsigte van ryker lewe. En dan kom daar . . .

Winter

Ons Here het die volheid daarvan ervaar; waarskynlik nie die volheid van die natuurlike elemente wat ons in die noordelike klimaat beleef nie, maar die seisoen van skynbare onvermoë om vrug te dra. Sommige het gesê: “Hy het ’n duiwel, en hy is mal; waarom luister julle na hom?” (Johannes 10:20). Op ’n tyd toe daar ’n fees van toewyding moes wees, “was dit winter.” Daar was ’n massiewe verdeeldheid onder die volk. Verwarring regeer oral. Jesus het net ’n blinde man genees, en die Jode het hom uit die tempel gewerp. Sulke vrugtelose en koue stowwerige harte bewoon die lande wat as “wit tot die oes” aangeteken is. Die ysgreep van sonde het die harte van die mensdom verhard, en die weivelde van godsdiens was begrawe onder blare van barre stoppels wat die oorblyfsels van leë doppe gedra het. Die geliefde dissipel het geen woorde vermors toe hy ons die feit gebring het dat . . . dit winter was.

“U het al die begrense van die aarde gereël; U het somer en winter gemaak” (Psalm 74:17).

Dit is maklik om te glo dat God die somer geskape het. Die deuntjies op ’n volmaakte sommerdag sing van die Goddelike tot ons. Die skoonheid wat oral om ons draai, getuig van Sy teenwoordigheid. Die opwekkende voëls in elke boom, die warmte van die aangename sonskyn, en die wonderbaarlike mirakel van die lewe trek ons harte na die Geeër toe deur duisend ongesiene filamentjies van lewe. Dit alles getuig van die waarheid dat “U het somer gemaak.”

Die dae van winter is anders. “Kan daar enige goeie ding uit Nasaret kom?” (Johannes 1:46). Ons deel soortgelyke gevoelens met dié van Natanël teenoor die wintermaande, want dit is nie so maklik om daar die hand van God te sien nie. Daar is baie lyding en verwerping wat ons binneste deurdring. Ek praat natuurlik nie van die seisoen in die natuur nie, maar van die lewensseisoene wat sy bestaan weerspieël. Ons doen goed om ons brose geloof te staaf met ’n stewige bekragtiging dat God ook die winter gemaak het, en dat ons nie aan Sy goddelike doelwitte daarin moet twijfel nie. Wat anders, behalwe ’n seisoen van verstikkende wanhoop en ongemak, kan ons apatiese siele wek tot . . .

Waardering

Afwesigheid laat die hart groter liefhê. So wek die koms van die winter ons waardering vir die somer. Ons sou blind wees as die somer voortdurend teenwoordig was. Dit is gepas gesê dat ons geliefdes net ons is wanneer ons hulle verloor het. Wanneer die winterseisoen uiteindelik hul laaste asem eis, begin ons hulle waardeer vir wie hulle werklik was. Dit is nie die man met oorvloed ononderbroke gesondheid wat die waarde van sy welstand die diepste voel nie. Daardie besef klop op sy stoep die dag wat sy gesondheid geknou word. Daar was baie rykes wat voorheen die skril leëheid van bankrotskap geken het. Dit het ’n onuitwiste merk in hul karakter ingeprent wat hulle geskik gemaak het vir die sukses wat daarna volg.

So sal die Christen dikwels ’n winterseisoen ervaar—’n tyd wanneer alles waarvoor hy geploeg het, na verlang en liefgehad het, latent lê onder die hopen van onvrugbare hooplose drifte. Johannes die Doper het dapper geprofeteer terwyl die visie vars was en die skare bymekaarkom om hom te hoor preek. Maar die donker en koue tronkcel was moeilik vir hom om te waardeer. Tog het God die winter gemaak, en hierdie seisoene in ons lewens is van primordiale belang vir ons geestelike welstand.

Versterking

In die 1700's het ’n vioolbouer met die naam Stradivari violiene geskep wat ongeëwenaard is in hul uitnemendheid van pragtige klank. Terwyl moderne kenners lank gepuzzeld was oor hul onvermoë om ’n soortgelyke instrument te skep, het die meeste besluite geneem dat die hout van daardie dae deur moeilike winters geverfde was, wat ’n kwaliteit voortgebring het wat in ons tyd nie gerepliseer kan word nie. Al die natuur strek onder die druk van die wintermaande, en die mens is nie uitgesonder nie. Die kort dae en die diep, koue nag plaas ’n groot eis op ons wil. In die somer is dit vergelykend maklik om by die aangewese uur uit die bed te kom. Die aarde is warm, die voëls sing besig, en die lig stroom deur die oop vensters. Maar in die donker van ’n ysige winteroggend, om die komberse af te gooi en in ’n triomfantelike gees op te staan, is ’n uitdagende onderneming. Dit vereis ’n vaste besluit om dit te bereik en laat baie goeie voornemens misluk.

Wanneer ons daardie gedagte verbreed om die mens se siel in te sluit, kom ons by ’n waarheid wat nie ontken kan word nie. Diegene wat die diep laste van harde lewe gedra het, het ’n aangebore krag in hul karakter ingeprent wat dié van milde omgewings nie kan begryp nie. Die morele karakter van Adonija het geknou, want “sy vader het hom nooit verweet op enige tyd in die sê: Waarom het jy so gedoen nie?” (1 Konings 1:6). Dit is die euwel van maklike lewe. Diegene wat hulleself aan alle kante sal isoleer teen die storm van die winter sal ongetwyfeld ’n verswakking van die wil ervaar. Diegene wat hul wil kan oorwin in die teenwoordigheid van ’n duidelik koue samelewing is op die pad na sukses. Somer is lui; maar winter maak ons besluitvaardig. Ons moet dinge doen selfs wanneer ons nie lus is om dit te doen nie. En so het God die winter gemaak.

Saamwees

“As twee bymekaar lê, dan hou hulle warmte: maar hoe kan ’n mens alleen warm wees?” (Prediker 4:11). Daar is geen behoefte aan so ’n saamwees in die somer nie—en geen begeerte daarvoor ook nie. Die krakende stoof het ’n hipnotiserende effek op die huishouding en meeste van ons winteraande draai om daardie vuur. Ons praat in dieselfde asem van gesin en huis, en dit is in die winter dat die kaggel gloei en liefde groei.

Daar is slegs oppervlakkige verhoudings onder dié wat geen swaarkry geken het nie. Dit verg die swaar soberheid van die winter om die genie van liefde in ons harte te bewerkstellig. Teëslag maak alles gelyk, terwyl wyse en eenvoudige mens saam trek in dieselfde juk. Gereeld, wanneer die dood sy koue vingers om ’n brose liggaam vou, skaar geliefdes by die bed. Vorige griewe word in die plechtigheid van die oomblik vergeet. Dit was by die poorte van die winter dat “Abraham die gees opgegee het, en in ’n goeie ouderdom gesterf het” (Genesis 25:8). Dit is hier dat die skeidende gordyne van die langdurige konflik tussen Isak en Ismael vervaag het en ’n gesamentlike poging tussen die twee broers hom “begrawe het in die grot van Machpela”.

Terwyl niemand van ons eens sal hoop op die politieke onrus wat vervolging en die verwydering van godsdienstige vryheid uit ons land sou meebring nie, is dit steeds my oortuiging dat ons vleeslike kerkverskeidings by die koms daarvan sal ophou. Dit verg winter om ons bymekaar te trek, en Christus was die voertuig waarop dit gery het. “Dit was winter. En Jesus het in die tempel in Salomo se voorhof geloop” (Johannes 10:23). Daar, voor die inhuldiging van Sy dood, het Sy dissipels almal gedroom van die hoofplek in die ry en gestreef om die grootste te wees. Nou, na die koue harde verwydering van die groen boom, is hulle almal gevind “met een gees in Salomo se voorhof” (Handelinge 5:12). Sulke is die bediening van die winter wat ons God ons gegee het.

Deernis

Om een of ander rede blyk dit dat ons ’n volle dosering van wanbehandeling moet ontvang voordat die deur van ons harte oopgesluit word vir gedagtes oor die hartseer lot van ander. ’n Mens kan net wonder wat die Goeie Samaritaan moes ervaar om so deurlopend ontroer te wees deur die toneel van die man in die sloot. Het die Jode nie elke nuwe dag ’n vars embleem van haat en veragtendheid op die doek van hulle bestaan geskilder nie? Vir sommige het die slegte behandeling de neiging om die hart te verhard. Hulle gaan deur die lewe in teruggetrokke wyse, met bitterheid en wraak in die roer van hul skip. Enige kennisse wat nie aan hulle diskriminasie voldoen nie, word gekategoriseer as verdag en vermy.

Daar is ander wat die koue steek van die winter verduur het en wantrou dat enigiemand dieselfde moet deurmaak. Hierdie harte word vinnig tot meegevoel aangevuur en dra bevooroordeelde simpatie teenoor diegene in soortgelyke nood. Selfs die ryk man wat sy winterse dood ontmoet het en nou in ewige hel was, is bewillig om genade te gee aan sy vyf broers wat op pad na dieselfde afgryslike bestemming was. Hoeveel meer behoort ons lome harte te roer tot liefde wanneer ons met sulke ongemak soos geestelike winter gekonfronteer word? Kan ons ons medemens groet met dieselfde strenge, ysige kyk wat ons in vorige dae in die gesig geslaan het? Is daar geen bewaarplek van barmhartigheid om uit te reik na die dwaalende siel wat die koue werklikheid van sy dwaasheid oes wat hy in sy jeug gesaai het nie?

Dit was winter in die dae toe ons Here in die tempel geloop het, en sekerlik is die geestelike omgewing vandag nie minder ysig nie. “Want omdat die boosheid vermenigvuldig sal word, sal die liefde van die meeste verkou” (Matteus 24:12). Diegene van ons wat kies om hierdie onvrugbare wildernis te versmaai, kan so teruggetrokke lewe soos ons begeer. Die res van ons sal gereed erkentlik wees dat ons God gemaak het . . . die winter en dit toelaat om sy volkome bewerking in ons harte te verrig.

'Tis winter now; the fallen snow
has left the heavens all coldly clear;
through leafless boughs, the sharp winds blow,
and all the earth lies dead and drear.

And yet God's love is not withdrawn;
his life within the keen air breathes;
his beauty paints the crimson dawn,
and clothes each branch with glittering wreaths.

And though abroad the sharp winds blow,
and skies are chill, and frosts are keen,
home closer draws her circle now,
and warmer glows her light within.

O God, you give the winter's cold,
as well as summer's joyous rays,
you warmly in your love enfold,
and keep us through life's wintry days.

Dirk scanned the sanctuary, trying to be discreet and yet utterly failing as he twisted and turned in his seat. He was intent on locating Brother Silas before the service began. Every Sunday morning, he would crane his neck in search of the hoary head of the fellowship’s oldest member, and every time his mother would cast Dirk that glance that meant, “Sit still and look forward.”

This morning, he didn’t have to even look behind him. Two rows from the front of the auditorium, Dirk spotted Brother Silas’ white hair and his black vest. To Dirk, it was a very special vest. In the pocket of that vest was something very important. In that vest pocket, there were mints. Lifesavers, to be exact. And all a little boy had to do to get one of those mints was to go up to Brother Silas after church service and politely ask to have one. And then, Brother Silas would smile, reach into the inner pocket, draw out a mint, and hand it to the little boy.

That was why Dirk diligently searched the church house to find Brother Silas’ whereabouts - so he would know where to go to get one of those mints. This Sunday was no different, and as soon as the last Amen was said, a swarm of young boys and girls began to cluster around Brother Silas like chickadees at a birdfeeder. Brother Silas genially doled out his mints in turn, all while continuing to chat with the men. When Dirk’s turn came, he dutifully said, “Thank you,” without even thinking what he said.

Dirk didn’t lose any time eating that mint, and before he knew it, the mint was gone and he could go on with his afternoon and with the rest of the week.

That Thursday, the phone rang, and when his mother picked it up, Dirk could tell that it was a recorded message announcing something because his mother only listened instead of holding up her end of the conversation. He didn’t think much of it until later in the evening when he overheard his parents discuss the message.

“What hospital did they say Brother Silas is in? Did they say how long they expect him to stay? Maybe we should make a visit,” Mother said.

“I think it would be worthwhile for us to pay him a visit,” replied Father.

“Will he be in church on Sunday?” interjected Dirk, stopping the travels of his tractor in his concern to hear the answer.

“No, I think it will be quite a while till he’ll feel able to be at church again. He’s very sick, Dirk,” Father said. Neither his father nor his mother expected the response that this answer caused. Dirk started crying, and at first, they were touched that he would be so compassionate about Brother Silas. And then Dirk started fussing.

“But what about my mint? If Brother Silas isn’t at church, I won’t get my mint! He just has to be at church!” He would have gone on and on in this way if his parents had let him.

“Why Dirk Phillips, first of all, we do not go to church services so that you can get a mint. We go to church services to worship God. Furthermore, you should be concerned about Brother Silas, not about whether you will get a mint or not. How would you like it if your friends were only concerned about something you gave them, without considering how you are doing?” “I’m sorry. I didn’t think about it like that,” Dirk sniveled, using his sleeve as a handkerchief.

“Can you think of anyone in the Bible who complained when they didn’t get what they wanted?” Mother inquired. No one came to Dirk’s mind, although he was sure that there were plenty of examples in the Bible. “The Israelites, Dirk. They often complained and it did not please God,” she prompted.

Father then asked Dirk to read through Numbers 11 and copy down the sentences that showed ungratefulness and how God felt about it. His parents then assured Dirk that they would look into visiting Brother Silas. They suggested planning to pick up a bag of mints on their way, just for Brother Silas.

When the day came to visit Brother Silas, Father took his son into the store to select a bag of mints. “Did you ever stop to think how many times Brother Silas has to do this to keep his pockets well lined with mints for all you children?” he asked Dirk, whose eyes grew wide at this little revelation.

“No, I never did. But he probably had to buy a whole bag every week! There’s a lot of us children at church.”

It was a full month before Brother Silas felt well enough to attend church services again. When he did, Dirk’s eyes lit up at the sight. At the close of the service, Dirk hung back for a while before approaching him. To be honest, he felt a little shy. But as he watched the other children receive their mints and he saw the unmistakable twinkle in Brother Silas’ eyes as he doled them out, Dirk grew more confident. He, too, joined the throng.

“I’m glad you’re feeling better, Brother Silas. I missed seeing you,” Dirk confided as he looked up into the face of the kindly gentleman.

“I am, too! It is very nice to be back. I quite missed being here,” replied Brother Silas, placing his hand gently on Dirk’s shoulder as they spoke. He then reached into his vest pocket and pulled out a mint. A Lifesaver, to be exact. And this time, when Dirk gave his thanks, it was with the feeling of gratitude and not just the words of it.

Dirk musterte das Gotteshaus und versuchte, unauffällig zu sein, scheiterte dabei aber völlig, während er sich im Sitz hin und her drehte. Er war darauf bedacht, Bruder Silas vor Beginn des Gottesdienstes zu finden. An jedem Sonntagmorgen reckte er den Hals auf der Suche nach dem ergrauten Haupt des ältesten Mitglieds der Gemeinschaft, und jedes Mal warf seine Mutter ihm diesen Blick zu, der so viel bedeutete wie: „Setz dich still hin und schau nach vorne.“

An diesem Morgen musste er nicht einmal nach hinten schauen. Zwei Reihen von der Vorderseite der Aula entdeckte Dirk Bruder Silas’ weiße Haare und seine schwarze Weste. Für Dirk war es eine ganz besondere Weste. In der Tasche dieser Weste befand sich etwas sehr Wichtiges. In dieser Westentasche lagen Pfefferminzbonbons. Genauer gesagt Lifesavers. Und alles, was ein kleiner Junge tun musste, um eines dieser Bonbons zu bekommen, war, nach dem Gottesdienst zu Bruder Silas zu gehen und höflich zu fragen, ob er eines haben dürfe. Dann würde Bruder Silas lächeln, in die Innentasche greifen, ein Bonbon hervorziehen und es dem Jungen überreichen.

Deshalb suchte Dirk eifrig im Gemeindehaus nach Bruder Silas, um zu wissen, wohin er gehen musste, um eines dieser Bonbons zu bekommen. Dieser Sonntag war keine Ausnahme, und sobald das letzte Amen gesprochen war, sammelte sich ein Schwarm kleiner Jungen und Mädchen um Bruder Silas wie Meisen an einem Vogelhäuschen. Bruder Silas verteilte seine Bonbons freundlich der Reihe nach, während er weiterhin mit den Männern plauderte. Als Dirk an der Reihe war, sagte er pflichtschuldig „Danke“, ohne überhaupt darüber nachzudenken, was er sagte.

Dirk verschwendete keine Zeit damit, das Bonbon zu essen, und ehe er sich versah, war das Bonbon weg und er konnte seinen Nachmittag und den Rest der Woche fortsetzen.

An diesem Donnerstag klingelte das Telefon, und als seine Mutter abnahm, merkte Dirk, dass es sich um eine aufgezeichnete Nachricht handelte, denn seine Mutter hörte nur zu, anstatt ein Gespräch zu führen. Er dachte nicht viel darüber nach, bis er später am Abend seine Eltern die Nachricht besprechen hörte.

„In welchem Krankenhaus haben sie gesagt, dass Bruder Silas ist? Haben sie gesagt, wie lange er bleiben wird? Vielleicht sollten wir ihn besuchen“, sagte Mutter.

„Ich denke, es wäre sinnvoll, wenn wir ihn besuchen würden“, erwiderte Vater.

„Wird er am Sonntag in der Kirche sein?“, unterbrach Dirk und hielt damit die Fahrt seines Traktors inne, weil er die Antwort hören wollte.

„Nein, ich denke, es wird eine ganze Weile dauern, bis er sich wieder in der Lage fühlen wird, in der Kirche zu sein. Er ist sehr krank, Dirk“, sagte Vater. Weder sein Vater noch seine Mutter erwarteten die Reaktion, die diese Antwort auslöste. Dirk begann zu weinen, und zunächst waren sie gerührt, dass er so mitfühlend gegenüber Bruder Silas war. Dann begann Dirk jedoch zu nörgeln.

„Aber was ist mit meinem Bonbon? Wenn Bruder Silas nicht in der Kirche ist, bekomme ich mein Bonbon nicht! Er muss einfach in der Kirche sein!“ Er wäre auf diese Weise weitergegangen, wenn seine Eltern ihn gelassen hätten.

„Warum, Dirk Phillips, erstens gehen wir nicht in den Gottesdienst, damit du ein Bonbon bekommst. Wir gehen zum Gottesdienst, um Gott anzubeten. Außerdem solltest du dir Sorgen um Bruder Silas machen, nicht darum, ob du ein Bonbon bekommst oder nicht. Wie würde es dir gefallen, wenn deine Freunde sich nur wegen etwas, das du ihnen gegeben hast, kümmern würden, ohne zu überlegen, wie es dir geht?“ „Es tut mir leid. Darüber habe ich nicht so nachgedacht“, schluchzte Dirk und benutzte seinen Ärmel als Taschentuch.

„Kannst du dich an jemanden in der Bibel erinnern, der sich beschwerte, wenn er nicht bekam, was er wollte?“, fragte Mutter. Dirk fiel niemand ein, obwohl er sicher war, dass es viele Beispiele in der Bibel gab. „Die Israeliten, Dirk. Sie beschwerten sich oft und das gefiel Gott nicht“, half sie ihm nach.

Vater bat dann Dirk, Numeri 11 durchzulesen und die Sätze abzuschreiben, die Undankbarkeit und Gottes Empfindungen darüber zeigten. Seine Eltern versicherten Dirk dann, dass sie sich darum kümmern würden, Bruder Silas zu besuchen. Sie schlugen vor, auf dem Weg eine Tüte Bonbons zu besorgen, nur für Bruder Silas.

Als der Tag gekommen war, an dem sie Bruder Silas besuchen wollten, nahm Vater seinen Sohn mit in den Laden, um eine Tüte Bonbons auszusuchen. „Hast du je darüber nachgedacht, wie oft Bruder Silas das wohl tun muss, damit seine Taschen für euch Kinder immer gut mit Bonbons gefüllt sind?“, fragte er Dirk, dessen Augen bei dieser kleinen Einsicht groß wurden.

„Nein, darüber habe ich nie nachgedacht. Aber er muss wohl jede Woche eine ganze Tüte kaufen! Bei uns Kindern in der Kirche sind es viele.“

Es dauerte einen ganzen Monat, bis sich Bruder Silas wieder so wohl fühlte, dass er den Gottesdienst besuchen konnte. Als er es dann tat, leuchteten Dirks Augen beim Anblick. Am Ende des Gottesdienstes blieb Dirk noch eine Weile zurück, bevor er auf ihn zuging. Um ehrlich zu sein, war er ein wenig schüchtern. Doch als er sah, wie die anderen Kinder ihre Bonbons bekamen und das unverkennbare Funkeln in Bruder Silas’ Augen, während er sie verteilte, wurde Dirk selbstbewusster. Auch er schloss sich der Menge an.

„Ich freue mich, dass es Ihnen besser geht, Bruder Silas. Ich habe es vermisst, Sie zu sehen“, vertraute Dirk ihm an, während er in das Gesicht des freundlichen Herrn aufschaute.

„Ich mich auch! Es ist sehr schön, wieder hier zu sein. Ich habe es wirklich vermisst“, antwortete Bruder Silas und legte dabei freundlich seine Hand auf Dirks Schulter, während sie sprachen. Dann griff er in seine Westentasche und zog ein Bonbon hervor. Genau genommen einen Lifesaver. Und dieses Mal, als Dirk seinen Dank aussprach, kam er mit dem Gefühl der Dankbarkeit und nicht nur mit den Worten davon.

City of God, how broad and far
outspread thy walls sublime!
The true thy chartered freemen are
of every age and clime:

One holy church, one army strong,
one steadfast, high intent;
one working band, one harvest-song,
one King omnipotent.

How purely hath thy speech come down
from man's primaeval youth!
How grandly hath thine empire grown
of freedom, love, and truth!

How gleam thy watch-fires through the night
with never-fainting ray!
How rise thy towers, serene and bright,
to meet the dawning day!

In vain the surge's angry shock,
in vain the drifting sands:
unharmed upon the eternal Rock
the eternal city stands.

And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter (John 10:22).

As the maddening winds howl about him, man turns his collar to the cold and damp. Little praise arises for the season that greets him at his weakest point and seeks to discomfort and discourage him from the zest of life. Winter settles in as a formidable authority and arouses anxiety not so much by the infliction of pain but the removal of the pleasant. As we cross the equinox, “the days get longer, and winter gets stronger”, states the old proverb, and it remains incisively correct.

Winter is the season of profound, persistent cold that drives the frost deeper and thickens the ice on the ponds. Man and beast battle its ferocity, and even the lifeless machinery rebels against winter’s adamant arrival. Chilly drafts penetrate every crack and crevice, forcing their heartless presence into the most private chambers. As the woodpiles shrink, utility bills increase in the struggle to resist winter’s array of armed forces. While a few gay tunes, such as Winter Wonderland, seek to capitalize upon its majestic moments, winter is generally despised by the normal inhabitants of this earth. We grimace under the menacing icy grip that holds us captive and longingly anticipate its eventual release.

Spring may have its equal share of soggy and uncomfortable appointments and ragged days. Northern tradition states that the robins must get snowed on three times before the full arrival of spring. But springtime is never void of the hope and glory of better days ahead. Summer can be unbearable with its burning heat and humidity, but it bears a semblance of blessed fruitfulness on every side, and few will slow their activities to notice its discomforts. The autumn days carry their nostalgic enchantment while the beauty of nature is painted in the most remarkable colors on the foliage of the landscape. The bounties of harvest provide an aura of rejoicing in their sheaves, and man’s heart is still merry with the prospects of maturing life. And then comes . . .

Winter

Our Lord experienced the fullness of it; probably not the fullness of the natural elements that those of us in the northern climates face, but the season of apparent fruitlessness. Some said, “He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?” (John 10:20). At a time when there was to be a feast of dedication, “it was winter.” There was a massive division among the people. Confusion reigned on every side. Jesus had just healed a blind man, and the Jews cast him out of the temple. Such fruitless and cold stony hearts inhabited the fields that were acclaimed to be “white unto harvest.” The icy grips of sin had hardened the hearts of humanity, and the meadows of religion were littered with barren stalks draped with the remains of empty husks. The beloved disciple wasted no words when he brought us the fact that . . . it was winter.

“Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter” (Psalm 74:17).

It is easy to believe that God has created summertime. The tunes on a perfect summer day sing to us of the Divine. The beauty revolving about us everywhere speaks of His presence. The cheering birds in every tree, the warmth of the pleasant sunshine, and the amazing prodigy of life draw our hearts to the Giver by a thousand invisible filaments of life. These all testify to the truth that “Thou hast made summer.”

The days of winter are different. “Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46). We share similar sentiments to those of Nathaniel toward the winter months, for it is not so easy to see the hand of God there. There is a great deal of suffering and rejection that we feel penetrating our inner man. I obviously speak not to the season within nature but to the seasons of life that parallel its existence. We do well to aid our frail faith by some solid affirmation that God has made winter, as well, and that we ought not to doubt His divine purposes in it. What, but a season of chilling despair and discomfort can arouse our apathetic souls to . . .

Appreciation

Absence makes the heart grow fonder. Thus does the advent of winter incite our appreciation for summer. We would be blind if summer were perpetually present. It has been aptly said that our dear ones are only ours when we have lost them. When the winter season finally claims their last breath, we then begin to appreciate them for who they really were. It is not the man with an abundance of uninterrupted health who feels most deeply the value of his well-being. That realization arrives on his doorstep the day his health is shattered. There have been many wealthy men who had previously known the stark bareness of bankruptcy. This indelibly embossed a permanent mark in their character that fitted them for the success that followed in its wake.

So the Christian will often experience a season of winter—a time when all that he had labored over, longed for and loved lies languishing beneath the mounds of sterile hopeless drifts. John the Baptist prophesied boldly while the vision was fresh and the crowds pressed around to hear him preach. But the dark and cold prison cell was difficult for him to appreciate. Yet, God has made winter, and these seasons in our lives are paramount to our spiritual well-being.

Strengthening

In the 1700s, a luthier by the name of Stradivari created violins unequaled in their excellence for beautiful sound. As modern experts puzzled long over their inability to create a similar instrument, most have resolved that the wood of the day had been seasoned by difficult winters, producing a quality that cannot be replicated in our day. All nature strains under the duress of the winter months, and man is not exempt. The short days and deep, brazen chill of the night apply a great demand upon our will. In summer, it is comparatively easy to get out of bed at the appointed hour. The earth is warm, the birds are busy singing, and the light is streaming through the open windows. But in the dark of a frigid winter morning, to fling back the covers and arise in a triumphant air is a challenging proposition. It demands a solid resolution to achieve and makes a failure out of many good intentions.

As we broaden that thought to encompass the soul of man, we reach a truth that cannot be denied. Those who have borne the deep burdens of hard living have an innate strength ingrained in their character that those of a mild environment cannot apprehend. The moral character of Adonijah had eroded, for “his father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so?” (1 Kings 1:6). This is the bane of easy living. Those who will insulate themselves on every side from the buffeting of winter will, no doubt, incur a weakening of the will. Those who can conquer their will in the presence of a blatantly cold society are on the highway to success. Summer is languid; but winter makes us resolute. We need to do things even when we don’t feel like doing them. And thus, God has made the winter.

Togetherness

“If two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone?” (Ecc. 4:11). There is no need for such togetherness in the summer—and no desire for it either. The crackling stove has a mesmerizing effect upon the household members and most of our winter evening activities center around it. We speak in the same breath, of hearth and home, and it is in winter that the hearth glows and love grows.

There are but shallow relationships among those who have known no hardship. It takes the heavy austerity of winter to perform the genius of love in our hearts. Adversity levels the playing field, while sage and simpleton pull together in the same yoke. Often, as death wraps its cold fingers around a frail body, loved ones rush to the bedside. Past grievances are forgotten in the solemnity of the moment. It was at the gates of winter that “Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age” (Genesis 25:8). It is here that the separating curtains of the long-standing conflict between Isaac and Ishmael abated and a joint effort between the two brothers “buried him in the cave of Machpelah”.

While none of us shall ever hope for the political unrest that would bring persecution and the removal of religious freedom from our land, it is still my belief that our carnal church divisions will cease upon its advent. It takes winter to pull us together, and Christ was the vehicle upon whom it rode in. “It was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon’s porch” (John 10:23). There, before the inauguration of His death, His disciples were all pushing for the head of the line and striving to be the greatest. Now, after the cold harsh removal of the green tree, they were all found to be “with one accord in Solomon’s porch” (Acts 5:12). Such is the ministry of winter that our God has gifted us with.

Sympathy

For some reason, it seems that we must receive a full dosage of maltreatment before the door of our hearts is unlocked to thoughts of the sorrowful plight of others. One can only wonder what the Good Samaritan must have experienced to be so thoroughly moved by the scene of the man in the ditch. Did not the Jews paint a fresh emblem of hatred and disdain before him on the canvas of each new day? For some, the ill-treatment has a tendency to harden the heart. These go through life in reclusive fashion, with bitterness and spite at the helm of their ship. Any acquaintances that remotely fail their discrimination are categorized as suspect, and avoided.

There are others who have endured the cold blast of winter and loathe that any should have to experience the same. These hearts are quickly aroused to pity and carry bias sympathy toward those of similar plight. Even the rich man who met his wintry death and was now in eternal hell was moved to extend mercy to his five brethren who were bound for the same dreadful destination. How much more should our sluggish hearts stir to charity when met with such discomforts as spiritual winter? Can we greet our fellow man with the same stern, icy glare that has smitten us in the face in bygone days? Is there no storehouse of mercy to extend to the wayward soul who is reaping the cold reality of his folly-filled life that he has sown in his youth?

It was winter in the days when our Lord walked in the temple, and surely, the spiritual environment today is no less frigid. “Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold” (Matthew 24:12). Those of us who choose to despise this barren wilderness can live reclusive at our will. The rest of us shall readily acknowledge that our God hast made . . . winter and allow it to have its perfecting work in our hearts.

“那时在耶路撒冷有修殿节，就是冬天。”（约翰福音 10:22）。

当恼人的寒风在他周围呼号，人便把衣领竖起以抵御寒湿。很少有人为在他最虚弱之时迎接他的季节唱赞美之歌；那季节寻求使他不适并使他对生命的热情灰心丧志。冬天像一个强有力的权威降临，令人不安，其激起焦虑的方式更多不是通过施以痛苦，而是通过剥夺那令人愉快之物。当我们越过昼夜平分点，正如古谚所说，“白天变长了，冬天却变得更冷”，这一点至今仍然一针见血。

冬天是深沉而持久的寒冷季节，冰霜渗得更深，池塘上的冰愈发厚重。人与畜与其凶猛搏斗，甚至无生命的机器也反抗冬天坚硬的到来。冷风钻入每一处缝隙，把无情的存在强加到最隐秘的房间里。随着木材堆的减少，为抵御冬天这支武装队伍而上升的燃料费用让人吃不消。虽然有几首欢快的小曲子，比如《冬日仙境》（Winter Wonderland），试图利用它的雄壮时刻，但普通的大多数地上居民仍然普遍厌恶冬天。我们在那威胁性的冰冷掌控下面露痛苦表情，渴望它最终的解除。

春天也许有它相等份额的潮湿与不适、以及参差不齐的日子。北方的传统说法是知更鸟在春天完全来临前必须被雪压到三次。但春日从不缺乏对更好日子的希望与荣光。夏天可能因灼热和湿度难以忍受，但周遭却处处显出蒙福的丰盈，很少有人会放慢脚步去注意它的烦恼。秋日带着怀旧的魅力，自然之美以最显著的色彩涂抹在景观的叶片上。收获的恩赐在麦束中提供了欢庆的气氛，人心仍因成熟生命的前景而喜乐。然后就来临了……

冬天

我们的主经历过它的丰满；也许不是我们这些在北方气候中所面对的自然要素的丰满，但那种显然的无果之季。有些人说，“他被鬼附着了，并且发狂；你们为甚么听他呢？”（约翰福音 10:20）。当那时要过修殿节的时候，“就是冬天。”人在各处严重分裂。混乱四处蔓延。耶稣刚治好一个瞎子，犹太人就把他赶出殿外。这样无果且冷酷的石心住在人们以为“白白的可以收成”的田野里。罪的冰冷把人类的心凝固了，宗教的草场遍布着空茎披着废弃外壳的残骸。当那位挚爱的门徒把事实告诉我们时，他没浪费字句……就是冬天。

“你安定了地的四极；你造夏与冬。”（诗篇 74:17）

人们很容易相信上帝造了夏天。完美夏日的乐曲向我们歌唱那位圣者。到处环绕我们的美景述说着他的同在。每棵树上欢快的鸟儿、宜人的阳光的温暖、以及生命这奇妙之举，以千条无形的生命细丝把我们的心拉向赐予者。这一切都证明了“你造了夏天”这一真理。

冬日却不同。“拿撒勒还能出什么好的吗？”（约翰福音 1:46）。我们对冬季有时抱着与拿但业相近的情感，因为在那儿不容易见到神的手。我们感受到大量的苦难与拒绝，渗透进我们的内心。我显然不是在谈论自然界的季节，而是与之相似的生命季节。我们最好用坚实的肯定来辅助我们脆弱的信心：上帝也造了冬天，我们不应怀疑他在其中的神圣旨意。那季节，除了冰冷的绝望与不适，又有什么能唤醒我们那冷漠的灵魂……

感恩

“久别情更浓。”因此冬天的来临激起我们对夏天的感激。如果夏天永远存在，我们将是瞎眼的。人们常说，当我们失去亲人时，他们才真正成为我们的；当冬季最终夺走他们的最后一口气，我们便开始为他们真实的样貌而感恩。并非那些拥有持续健康的人最深切体会到健康的价值；那种觉悟是在他健康被摧毁的那一天来到他家门口。许多曾经富有的人，先前都尝过破产的赤裸清贫。这在他们性格上留下了不可磨灭的印记，使他们适合后来随之而来的成功。

基督徒常要经历一个冬季——一个他所劳作、渴望并所爱的一切都在无生气的绝望雪堆下萎靡不振的时期。施洗约翰在异象新鲜、众人围着听他讲道时曾大胆地先知。但那黑暗、寒冷的监牢对他来说是难以感恩的。然而，上帝造了冬天，我们生命中的这些季节对于我们的属灵健康至关重要。

坚固

在十八世纪，一位名叫斯特拉迪瓦里的制琴师造出的提琴在优美音色上无与伦比。现代专家为无法造出同类乐器而苦思良久，大多数人认为当时的木材经受了严冬的调节，产生了今人无法复制的品质。万物在冬季的压迫下受难，人亦不例外。短日与漫长、厚重的夜寒对我们的意志提出了极大挑战。夏天，按约定时分起床相对容易。大地温暖，鸟儿忙着歌唱，光透过开着的窗户。然而在冰冷的冬日清晨，要掀开被子并以凯旋的姿态起身，是个困难的命题。它要求坚定的决心去成就许多美好的意向，否则便成了失败。

当我们把这个思想扩展到人的灵魂上，我们就得出一个不可否认的真理。那些承受过艰苦生活重担的人，他们性格中根植着一种内在的力量，是温和环境中的人无法体会的。亚多尼雅的道德品格已经消蚀，因为“他父亲从来没有在任何时候责备他说：你为何行这样事呢？”（列王记上 1:6）。这就是安逸生活的祸根。那些四面用保护层包裹自己以免受冬天冲击的人，无疑会招致意志的衰弱。能够在明显冷酷的社会中征服自己意志的人，才走在通往成功的路上。夏天使人懈怠；但冬天使我们坚决。我们需要在不想做的时候仍然去做。因此，上帝造了冬天。

同在

“两个人同睡就暖和；独睡怎能温暖呢？”（传道书 4:11）。夏天不需要这样的亲近，也没人渴望它。炉火的噼啪声对家庭成员有着催眠的作用，我们大多数的冬夜活动都围绕着它展开。我们常把“炉边”和“家”连在一起说，正是在冬天炉火闪耀，爱意增长。

那些未曾经历艰难的人彼此之间的关系往往很浅薄。正是冬日的严峻造就出心中爱的天才。逆境使人站在同一水平，智者与愚者往往一同扛起同样的担子。常常，当死亡将它冰冷的手指缠绕在孱弱的身上，亲人就匆匆赶到床边。先前的怨恨在那庄严的一刻被忘却。正是在临近冬天之门时，“亚伯拉罕气绝，年纪老迈，死了”（创世记 25:8）。正是在这里，长期的以撒与以实玛利之间的纷争的分隔帷幕退却，兄弟二人联手把他“葬在马革波设的洞里”。

尽管我们无人会希望有那种会带来迫害并剥夺我们国家宗教自由的政治动乱，但我仍然相信，当冬日来临时，我们属肉体的教会分裂会停止。冬天把我们拉到一起，而基督就是那载着它来临的工具。“就是冬天。耶稣在所罗门的廊下，在殿里行走。”（约翰福音 10:23）。在那里，在他受死就要开始之前，门徒们都在争先恐后，努力争取首位与卓越。现在，在那绿树被寒霜残酷除去之后，他们却都“同心合意在所罗门的廊下”（使徒行传 5:12）。这就是上帝赐给我们的冬日事工。

同情

不知为何，我们似乎必须先接受一剂又一剂的虐待，心门才会为他人的悲惨遭遇而打开。人不禁要想，那好撒马利亚人必须经历过什么，才会被路旁那人那样彻底地感动？犹太人在他面前每日是否未曾在画布上重新描绘出仇恨与轻视的徽记？对某些人来说，虐待会使心变硬。这些人以隐居的方式度日，心中掌握着苦毒与怨恨。任何稍微不合他们标准的熟人都会被视为可疑并被回避。

还有些人曾忍受过冬天的冷冽，厌恶任何人也要经历同样的遭遇。这些人的心很快被怜悯唤醒，对处于相似困境的人抱有偏袒的同情。即便那位在冬日死去、如今在永恒地狱中的富人，也感动要向他的五个将往同一可怕去处的弟兄施以怜悯。我们在属灵冬天来临时，慵懒的心又当何等更应被慈悲激动？我们能否以曾在昔日打在我们脸上的那种严厉、冰冷的目光来迎接我们的同胞？对那在青春年少时播种愚行而今正收获冷现实的迷失灵魂，我们没有一仓的怜悯可施吗？

当主在殿里行走的日子是冬天，今天的属灵环境也无疑同样严寒。“因为不法的事增多，许人的爱心才渐渐冷淡了。”（马太福音 24:12）。我们当中那些选择鄙弃这荒凉旷野的人可以随意隐居。其余的人则会坦然承认我们的神造了……冬天，并让它在我们心中成就祂完备的工作。
